Annotated by Vinaya Master Hongyi
Revised by his junior Daguang

blocks.text: Prefatory Note by Vinaya Master Hongyi

inline.s: The Venerable Master Jianyue (an account of the Venerable Master Jianyue is also to be found in the Gazetteer of Baohua Mountain and the Records of Pure Land Sages and Worthies; his age in the world was seventy-nine), in all his dealings with people and in everything he did throughout his life, bore a severe and commanding air, never revealing any warmth of kindness. Perhaps some would think him excessively stern and unfeeling. Yet most of the good spiritual friends of this Dharma-ending age have no firmness of bone in them at all; they drift and mingle with worldly custom and worldly habits, and then call themselves ‘skilful in means, compassionate in accommodating the world,’ to conceal what they are. The words and deeds of the Venerable Master as set out in this book are precisely the right medicine for that disease. The Confucians say: ‘When men hear of the character of Bo Yi, the stubborn grow upright and the timid find resolve’ (hearing of the noble character of Bo Yi, even the stubborn become honest and upright, and even cowards set up a firm and lofty ambition). I think this applies equally to the Venerable Master Jianyue. On the fifth day of the ninth month I finished compiling the outline of the Master’s chronological biography, then collated A Wandering Talk of a Dream, added and revised the headings, key points, and annotations, and wrote this prefatory note. On the thirteenth day of the ninth month I finished the two pieces of ‘Separate Records from My Informal Lectures.’ Lying in bed, I called to mind the past affairs of Elder Jianyue and made a vow to go next year to Mount Hua (Baohua Mountain) to pay homage at the Master’s memorial pagoda. Before I knew it my tears were falling in streams, and I felt deeply how the vitality of the Buddha’s gate has withered and declined — the grief pierced me to the marrow.

Some years ago, in a catalogue of the scriptural canon, I once saw A Wandering Talk of a Dream listed. Taking it for a popular Buddhist book written by a man of our own day to exhort the world, I borrowed a copy and began to read, and only then learned that it was the Ming-dynasty Vinaya Master Jianyue of Baohua Mountain’s own account of the ascetic deeds of his pilgrimage and his visits to teachers. I was delighted and leaped for joy, feeling it to be incomparably precious, and read it over and over until I forgot even to eat. In the reading I was deeply inspired, and was moved to shed tears dozens of times. Therefore I summarized the meaning section by section, added marginal notes, and, consulting maps, drew a chart of the Master’s pilgrimage route (note: this text is taken from the internet, and the chart is not appended), so as to lessen the difficulties of students who later study this work.

On the tenth day of the eighth month of the jiaxu year (1934) I finished reading it. On the twenty-fifth day I finished making a copy and wrote this prefatory note, by Hongyi at the Jinshui Hermitage.
[Hongyi (

)] A great monk of the Republican period who restored the Nanshan Vinaya school. A native of Pinghu in Zhejiang, his secular surname was Li, his given name Guanghou, his style Shutong. Before leaving home he was a man of many talents, accomplished in poetry, song, prose, calligraphy, painting, and seal carving, in not one of which was he unskilled. After leaving home his dharma name was Yanyin and his style Hongyi; he devoted himself to spreading the Nanshan Vinaya school, and the world called him Vinaya Master Hongyi.

inline.s: In the winter of the jiayin year of the Kangxi reign (

), the ācāryas (masters of conduct, that is, teachers who instruct disciples so that their conduct is upright and proper, and who are themselves fit to be a model for their disciples; that is, guiding teachers) such as Liyan, together with the heads of the various ranks and the officers of the monastery, reverently and earnestly begged me to relate the course and the deeds of my pilgrimage and my visits to teachers, so as to encourage those who come after. And so I took up the brush and, from beginning to end, set it all down in a rough and undecorated way, without literary polish.

I am a son of the Xu family of Chuxiong Prefecture in Yunnan. When I was fourteen my two younger brothers were still small, and to our misfortune our father and mother died one after the other. The three brothers were left alone and helpless, with no one to rely on. My uncle was advanced in years and had no son of his own; he lavished affection on us and raised and taught us with kindness. At that time I once copied a portrait of Bodhisattva Guanyin, and everyone praised me as a little Wu Daozi.
By nature I loved to roam and see the sights, never letting my feet be still. In the sixth year of the Tianqi reign (

), when I was fifteen, I heard that on the border between Dali Prefecture and Beisheng Prefecture there was a Jinsha River, and that the people living along its banks made their living by panning the sands for gold. So I invited two or three companions and walked five hundred li to see it for myself, and when I saw how things actually stood, I marveled that the great earth in its creating and nourishing of living beings should have such a way as this. I also heard that Heqing Prefecture lies among a host of mountains, the mountain shapes standing up sheer like walls, with the rivers level and the roads across the flats perilous and hard. In ancient times a dragon of former karma wished to turn it into a sea. The land in the southeast there is low and sunken, and is called Dianwei; when the waters reach that point they gather and are blocked, and gradually would have flooded over. There was an Indian monk of spirit, the Venerable Magadha, who in compassion would save living beings; with his tin staff he bored several tens of holes at the foot of the mountains of Dianwei, more than five li deep, and led the standing water into the Jinsha River. Here I met the scholar Xiao Anchu of Langqiong County. He had once invited me at Chuxiong to paint a portrait of Bodhisattva Guanyin for him, and when we met he was overjoyed and invited me to go to Langqiong County. Then the provincial graduate Yang Shaoxian and others came to call on me as well. Xiao Anchu and Yang Shaoxian were relatives, both families of great wealth, each with famous gardens and villas, and our temperaments agreed; and so I stayed there five years.

In my twenty-seventh year, which was the first year of the Chongzhen reign, in the first third of the twelfth month, I was gathered with several good friends at the Plum Garden for pleasure. This garden lies twenty li from Langqiong County town and was the site of Xiao Anchu’s study; it backs onto Mount Shibao, covers more than ten mu, and has several hundred pear trees planted in it, so that flowers of every kind may be enjoyed in all four seasons. When our merry drinking and laughing were at their height, I received a letter from my old home, telling me that my uncle had been looking forward to my return. He had died just after his seventieth birthday, without waiting to see me once more. At once I was utterly shaken; the wine left me, and I wept in grief. I had never believed in Buddhism or Daoism, yet now all at once the thought of leaving home arose in me, and I said to my friends: ‘I have truly been unfilial: the kindness of my parents and my uncle has gone unrequited, and the sin of the greatest impiety is hard to escape. Now I am resolved to leave home, to expiate my guilt and repay their kindness. From this parting we shall not gather again.’ When they heard this, their eyes went wide as they stared at me, thinking I had gone mad.

Xiao Anchu said: ‘You cannot go a single day without wine — how is it you speak of leaving home and eating vegetarian food? If you would leave home, there is no need to go elsewhere: I will make you a gift of this garden to cultivate in.’ Yang Shaoxian said: ‘Since Brother Xiao is making a gift of the garden, everything you need for daily use I shall undertake to supply, and I will give you my own houseboy as well, to serve you as you please.’ I said: ‘These four things have happily been brought to fulfilment by you two gentlemen; it must be a good connection from many lives past. Yet I would ask further that from now on you bring no meat or wine into this garden. Firewood and rice need not be limited in quantity. And any monk or Daoist on pilgrimage, I wish to provide with a vegetarian meal.’ They both gladly agreed, with not the least difficulty.

Twenty li from the garden stood a Daoist temple, and I went to visit it and told of my wish to leave home. An old Daoist priest there wanted to talk me into becoming his disciple. Seeing that his bearing had neither dignity nor rule, and that his talk was unreasonable, I said I would go back and think it over and then reply. I noticed a copy of the Imperial Scripture enshrined on his desk and wished to take it back to the garden to read. He said: ‘You are not a Daoist — how can you speak so casually of requesting a scripture!’ At once I took off the clothes I was wearing and exchanged them with him for a Daoist robe. He said: ‘Since you are truly leaving home, you may take it.’ I returned to the garden and enshrined the scroll upon the desk, bowed and paid it reverence, and changed my own name to Zhenyuan, with the style Huanji.

When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month came, I wrote out a tablet to the Jade Emperor and set it up for offering, and with utmost sincerity called upon the divine names and bowed in worship. By the middle of the night my spirit was somewhat weary, and before I knew it I had fallen asleep kneeling and bowed to the ground. I dreamed that the vast blue sky was as clear as if washed, and a red sun shone on high. I came before a great temple, its halls and terraces high and broad and grand, surrounded outside by red walls, with pines and cypresses in ordered rows, and in the middle a gate. I saw many monks inside, all with shaven heads and wearing sanghatis. My heart was glad, and I wanted to go in, but the threshold was too high to step over. I struggled and tried several times, and suddenly I was inside. Once in, I felt that I was no longer a Daoist but had the likeness of a monk. I saw that amid the circle of monks there was a high seat, and on it sat two old monks dressed in red, who smiled and beckoned me to come up. So I pushed my way through the monks and went up. The old monk took a scroll of scripture and gave it to me, saying: ‘You shall expound it for the assembled monks.’ I took it, stood beside the seat, and began to preach, and all the monks knelt on the ground to listen.

When I woke from that sleep my whole body was streaming with sweat, and what I had preached I had utterly forgotten. Then I thought: in the end I am not a man of the Daoist gate; hereafter I must surely become a monk of the Buddha’s gate. The day broke upon the second year of Chongzhen, and I was twenty-eight. From then on I knelt and recited the Imperial Scripture once each day, and every third day I bowed in repentance for a week to atone for my transgressions; and each time I made dedication and prayer, I wept and sobbed, declaring that I would repay their kindness. When old acquaintances and good friends came to the garden to share in the merit, they saw that my former worldly air was wholly gone and that I cultivated in earnest without the least slackness, and they all gave rise to faith and praised me without end; some made a vow to eat vegetarian for life, and some wished to shake off the dust and leave home. From that time, within a hundred li, everyone knew that the Xiao family’s Plum Garden had a Daoist named Huanji.

Eighty li from Langqiong County town there is a town called Sanying, where stands the Great Enlightenment Temple, which had set the spring of the third year of Chongzhen for the opening of a Dragon Flower Dharma Assembly. So I went at the Lantern Festival to share in the merit, and it happened that the presiding monk, Master Yunguan, and the various heads of the assembly who were preparing the Dharma assembly were all in the great hall. When I had composed my bearing and bowed to the Buddha, I entered the refectory and sat down. A layman with white hair and a scholar’s cap came forward, joined his palms in greeting, and asked me where I had come from. I said: ‘From Langqiong.’ He asked: ‘Have you met the Daoist Huanji of the Xiao family’s Plum Garden? How are his resolve for the Way and his cultivation?’ I said: ‘I have met him; the man is worth hearing of by name only, not worth meeting. He makes a show of cultivation, when in truth he parades an empty reputation and deludes the crowd. And besides, he has not been a monk long — what moral cultivation could he have to speak of!’ The old layman’s face darkened, and he said gravely: ‘Since you are a man who cultivates the Way, when you see virtue in another you should praise it, and when you know of another’s fault you should conceal it kindly. To be so jealous of a fellow cultivator on the same path — how can you call yourself a man who cultivates the Way?’

Just then a layman came in from outside; he knew me, and greeted me with delight. Seeing this, the old layman asked him: ‘Do you know this Daoist?’ He answered: ‘This is Master Huanji of the Xiao Garden.’ The old layman said: ‘I very nearly missed him to his face!’ He at once told the presiding monk and the various heads of the assembly, and together they bowed to me and asked after me, and earnestly begged me to preside over the altar. I said: ‘One who presides over a Dragon Flower altar ought to be thoroughly versed in the rites of the Mysterious Gate; I only practice quiet cultivation and devote myself to bowing and recitation, and am not fit for it.’ Again and again they pressed their sincere request without cease, and again and again I declined. In the end, seeing that their feeling was firm and hard to refuse, I said: ‘For so great a Dharma assembly, providing vegetarian meals for the monks must be the foremost task. Have you made preparation for it?’ They answered: ‘We have made none.’ I said: ‘If this one matter of vegetarian meals for the monks is lacking, how can it be called a victorious assembly! This task I will do my utmost to undertake. First, that together with the laymen I may adorn the bodhimanda; second, that I may guide all the faithful in giving alms and planting blessings.’ Hearing this, they were delighted and bowed in thanks.

The next day I prepared to visit the notable men of the town and urge them to take the lead in supporting this Dharma assembly. Someone said that in this town there was a family named Ai, local gentry, and another family named Lü, an officer holding the rank of commander. The two families were joined in marriage, father-in-law and son-in-law, both wealthy households and both fond of doing good works, and moreover close kin of Xiao Anchu of Langqiong County; beyond them there was no one to compare with them. I thought this matter looked promising, and decided to call first at the Lü house. At the gate I happened to meet the man Xiao Anchu had sent with gifts, so I asked him to announce me as well. I was invited in, and it happened that Protector of the Dharma Ai was there too; he had heard of me but had never met me. I told him of the matter of providing vegetarian meals for the monks at the assembly. Protector Ai said: ‘Where is the sense in holding a Dragon Flower Dharma Assembly without feeding the monks? Since Master Huanji is willing to shoulder this matter alone, this old man too is willing to take the lead in promoting it.’ He at once sent men to invite the virtuous and respected men and the faithful of the town to come and discuss it together, and all were glad to follow.

The next day the two Dharma protectors Ai and Lü carried two canopies, one blue and one yellow, to left and right, while I in my Daoist robe and straw sandals walked between them, and the village elders and the faithful followed behind, and we made a circuit of the great and small streets and lanes of the town, each of us urging friends and kin to join in the good work. The money and goods contributed that day came to more than three hundred taels of silver and coin, and more than five hundred dan of rice.

Back at the temple, we at once hired craftsmen and put up several tens of thatched huts; all the other furnishings and utensils were borrowed from each household. Only in the matter of managing the kitchen was it very hard to find a suitable man. In the afternoon a monk on pilgrimage came, of plain and antique appearance, his speech gentle yet forceful. Asked where he came from, he said he had just come from paying homage at Mount Jizu, and that he was a man of Xundian Prefecture and his dharma name was Chengzhuo. I asked him to help, and he agreed at once. He had a strong resolve for the Way; he laboured day and night with no trace whatever of slackness or weariness, and he and I became companions of one mind on the same path. Every day the cloud-and-water monks and Daoists who came to the assembly for the vegetarian meal numbered no fewer than a thousand, and the orphaned and widowed, men and women, beggars and the poor, were more than a hundred. Every benefactor who came to set out a meal for the monks I urged to bow to the assembly and seek blessing. And I further taught them, saying: among these poor and suffering people there may well be fathers and mothers and kin of ours from many lives past. Because in former lives they did not make offerings to the Three Jewels and did not relieve the poor and suffering, they have drawn down such retribution in this life. You and I are all fleshly eyes and ordinary men, and cannot see this; we should break down the habit of pride and arrogance and bow in reverence. They heard it and all believed, and did as they were told. This was a thing rarely seen in the region south of Yunnan since ancient times, and it was also a cause of teaching and guidance that I made out of my own intention, unlearned in the scriptures as I was. When the assembly was about to end, I heard the heads of the assembly discussing privately that they would prepare gifts to thank me. On the day before the assembly was to conclude, I privately took leave of Chengzhuo alone, and before the sky grew light, quietly went back alone to Langqiong County.
In the fourth year of Chongzhen (

) I was thirty. In the middle of the second month, in Jianchuan Prefecture there were two brothers, Li Junfu and Li Junbi, both famous scholars of the literati, firm believers in the Three Jewels, who often met with me. They had a study more than thirty li from Jianchuan Prefecture town, where the green pines were ancient and the red cliffs wonderfully fair, and extremely secluded; and they wished to invite me there for quiet cultivation. The two of them were on very close terms with Xiao Anchu, so they sent a man with a letter to Anchu. Anchu was at first irresolute: to speak in terms of the affection of fellow cultivators, it was hard for him to part from me; to speak in terms of the friendship of Confucian scholars, he ought to grant the Li brothers’ request. And so he was caught in two minds. I said that this place was not far from Jianchuan, and that it would be better to put others before myself. So I took leave of the Xiao Garden and accepted the invitation to the Li Garden. I arrived on the fifteenth day of the third month, and there I fed the monks as before, and cultivated with even greater diligence. The Li brothers grew in faith, and the elder brother too roused his mind to eat vegetarian for the rest of his life.

In the beginning of the sixth month the weather was hot, and to escape the heat I climbed up onto the red cliff and, finding a great rock, sat cross-legged upon it. Looking west, I saw that perhaps five li away, amid encircling mountains and dense and flourishing woods, there must surely be an ancient temple. So I rose and walked toward it. Reaching the place, I saw only a thatched hut, its bamboo door half closed, with the sound of a wooden fish

and of murmured sutra recitation coming from within. When the sound of the sutra ceased, I went in and saw an old monk of venerable appearance, and I bowed to him. He said: ‘You of the yellow caps (Daoists) mostly do not bow to monks. Where do you come from, and what is your name?’ I said I was Huanji of the Xiao Garden in Langqiong, and that I was now invited to stay at the Red Cliff study. He clasped his hands in greeting and said: ‘I have heard that Master Huanji, at the Dragon Flower Assembly in Sanying, fed the monks and relieved the poor without distinguishing between schools or between noble and base, and that he was good at instructing benefactors and the faithful to empty themselves of the mark of self. May I ask whom you took as your teacher, and what scriptures and teachings you read, that you could perform so great a Buddha-work?’

I said: ‘I have never taken a teacher, nor have I recited or read the scriptures and teachings of the Buddha’s gate; I did it all simply according to my own intention.’ He was rather astonished, and said: ‘What you have done is altogether the conduct of a bodhisattva. You have great roots of wisdom; quickly take a clear-understanding monk of high rank as your teacher and shave your head and become a monk, so that you may spread the Buddha-Dharma and guide living beings. I constantly recite the Avatamsaka Sutra; you may take it and read it reverently on your knees. The principles of Buddhism and Daoism have shallow and deep among them, but the compassionate vows and the conduct of a bodhisattva are immeasurable and boundless. You will of yourself give rise to the bodhi mind, without needing to rely upon another’s instruction.’ When I heard this I bowed in thanks, requested the Avatamsaka Sutra, and returned to the Red Cliff. There I burned incense and read it on my knees until I had finished the chapter ‘The Wondrous Adornments of the World Rulers,’ and then I recalled the dream I had had at night when I first left home. The wish to shave my head and become a monk suddenly grew urgent within me.

At the end of the seventh month the presiding monk of the Great Temple of Langqiong County, Miaozong, brought a letter from Xiao Anchu and came to see me, inviting me to go with him on pilgrimage to Mount Jizu. This was just what I wished, so I at once took leave of the Li brothers, and joining Anchu and Miaozong, reached the mountain on the fifteenth day of the eighth month and lodged for the night at Jiguang Temple. Asking whether there were any clear teachers in the mountain, I heard that on Lion Peak there were two old monks, Dali and Baiyun, who cultivated the pure karma with great diligence and had not come down the mountain in thirty years. So on the eighteenth I went with Miaozong and Anchu, threading the pine woods, skirting the stream paths, descending into the valleys, and climbing the sheer cliffs, until we reached their quiet hut, where I bowed and begged them to shave my head for me. The old monk Dali questioned me in detail about my background and my reasons, and was so kind as to consent, ordering me to prepare robe and bowl. Anchu said: ‘Since the Master has been so compassionate as to accept Huanji, his robe, bowl, and provisions shall all be borne by me, your disciple.’ The old monk Baiyun said: ‘I observe that this man will in the end become a great vessel of the Buddha’s gate; we must not act hastily. I fear that leaving home is easy, but that keeping the precepts may not be firm. He must go from door to door begging alms himself, to break down his habit of pride, and to test his resolve. When he has begged the robe and bowl, then let him come back to the mountain and be shaved.’ I thought to myself that of these two good spiritual friends, one accepted me in compassion and the other would break down my pride and arrogance — truly they inspired awe and reverence. The Buddha’s gate is altogether different from the Mysterious Gate (Daoism): it is careful and does not let things run loose. Knowing that the time was not yet ripe, I said with tears in my eyes: ‘I shall follow the Master in every point you have spoken. But since I have climbed the mountain and come to this place, I cannot bear to return empty-handed. I beg the Master in his compassion to grant me one dharma name. Though I am not yet shaved, let me for the time being be a monk in heart.’ When the old monk Dali heard this, his face broke into a smile, and he gave me the dharma name Shuqiong.

After bowing, I withdrew. My heart was wondering what I ought to do next, and while I was still hesitating, a monk named Yuefeng came up and asked me: ‘Daoist, what is it in your heart that you cannot settle?’ I said: ‘I am just wondering where to go to beg for robe and bowl; there is no place I know.’ He said: ‘Setting out from Langqiong County and crossing Mount Fengwei, two hundred li on there is a place called Luomajing, where they produce salt; there are several tens of thousands of households, fond of good and mostly wealthy. I am a man of that place. In a few days I mean to go back to pay my respects to my teacher. I imagine you have never been there, so you may come along with me.’ At the end of the ninth month I left Mount Jizu with Yuefeng and set out for Fengwei, and only after more than half a month’s walking did we reach Luomajing, where we stayed at the Fangguang Temple on the western mountain. The presiding monk, Wuzong, received us with delight, as though we were not meeting for the first time. This temple was the family shrine of the Yang Xiong clan; the family had delighted in good works and almsgiving for generation after generation, and most of the younger sons and nephews followed the calling of Confucian scholars. Together with the praise and encouragement of the two masters Yuefeng and Wuzong, the faithful all came to help; and there was also a local native official named Ziyan, who met me once and took to me greatly, so that we held each other in much affection and respect.

What had been a strange place when I arrived became instead a place of warm familiarity. I was urgent to return to Mount Jizu to be shaved, yet again and again I was pressed to stay by the faithful benefactors of the place. In the beginning of the ninth month of the fifth year of Chongzhen (

), an old Dharma Master Liangru of the provincial capital was invited to Yongchang County to expound the scriptures, and on his way back to the capital after the completion of the lectures he happened to pass this way and stayed at the Great Enlightenment Temple on the eastern mountain. So I discussed it with Yuefeng, saying: ‘The faithful benefactors here hold me firmly and will not let me go, and my resolve to leave home is not yet fulfilled. I mean to receive the shaving from the old Dharma Master Liang so that I may attend upon him and study; but I fear that in doing so I shall go against my original vow to be shaved on Mount Jizu, and break faith with the old monk Dali. What is to be done?’ Yuefeng said: ‘I know that Master Liang belongs to the line of Jiguang Temple and was abbot of Jiguang Temple for three years; your dharma name too belongs to the Jiguang lineage. If you receive the shaving from Master Liang, it may look as though you have left Mount Jizu, but in terms of the dharma lineage you would still be a dharma-grandson of the old monk Dali, and it cannot be counted a breach of faith — indeed it fulfils your original vow. You should do it at once, and not hesitate any longer.’ Only then did I make up my mind. So Yuefeng and I left Fangguang Temple, went down the western ridge and up to the Great Enlightenment Temple on the eastern mountain, where I bowed to Master Liangru, saying only that I had come to pay my respects and make offering, not daring to speak out bluntly and ask for the shaving. Through the Master’s gracious consent I moved to stay at Fangguang Temple on the western mountain.

Early the next morning I burned incense and earnestly begged Dharma Master Liangru to shave my head for me. Master Liangru laughed and said: ‘Last night I dreamed of a monk wearing a sanghati, with a countless following, who said to me that his hair had grown long and asked me to shave it off for him. Today that cause and condition has come to pass. You are one who has come again; you can carry on my work of spreading the Dharma and benefiting beings. You should be given the name Dubi, with the style Shaoru. First choose an auspicious day, prepare the five robes, and receive the five fundamental precepts.’ I grieved deeply that I had left home so late, yet I rejoiced that I had deep causes from former lives. So we divined and fixed the fifth day of the tenth month for the shaving. On that day the faithful men and women of the streets came up the mountain to the temple in an unbroken stream to share in the merit. I was fretting over the lack of helpers when, strolling out of the temple gate, I ran straight into Chengzhuo. Two years had passed since we parted at Sanying town, and meeting today was like a tryst arranged long beforehand. Asked where he had come from, he said: ‘From Baotai Mountain in Yongchang Prefecture, to attend upon the old Dharma Master Liang. Last night I came to the foot of the mountain and heard that the Master was at Fangguang Temple and was today to shave a Daoist — so it was you, Master Huanji!’ We both laughed aloud; truly it was an inconceivable and wondrous connection. At the hour of Si (between nine and eleven in the morning) the Dharma seat was set out and the ceremony of shaving and receiving the precepts was held. Many men and women crowded around the seat to watch, as though beholding their nearest kin, sighing and lingering, unable to bear to leave; only when the meal offering was done did they disperse, and all along the road nothing was heard but the unbroken sound of the Buddha’s name.

The next evening Yuefeng said: ‘Many of the faithful of this place recite the sutras, yet they have never once heard a Dharma Master expound them. If Master Shao is willing to undertake the lecturing, and the old Dharma Master Liang in his compassion consents, then the connection of having been shaved in this place will never be forgotten. Who, when he is truly hungry and meets with fine food, would not wish to eat his fill!’ So I reported Master Yuefeng’s proposal to the old Dharma Master Liangru and said that I was willing to act as the period-master. The Master allowed me to lecture on the Lotus Sutra. We began on the tenth day. During the lecture period, all the furnishings and utensils used in the place were borrowed from the native official Ziyan, and the money and rice for daily use were contributed voluntarily by the common people. By day I acted as period-master, lecturing and also serving as guest-prefect to receive visitors; by night I studied the text, and the next day I took the seat and expounded it. The storekeeping and internal affairs I entrusted to Master Chengzhuo, and all outside purchasing was decided by Master Yuefeng. Each day the four assemblies who came to hear the sutra were very many, and the three meals of gruel and vegetarian dishes never ran short. On the eighth day of the twelfth month the lectures were brought to a close, with money and rice to spare, which both benefited living beings and increased their faith.

On the ninth day I took leave of the various benefactors and Dharma protectors, and on the tenth I set out with my Master, arriving in Langqiong County on the fifteenth and staying at Miaozong Temple. Xiao Anchu was away on a long journey and I did not see him; when Yang Shaoxian learned of our arrival he received us at his academy, where we settled for the summer and passed the New Year. There was a fellow cultivator on the path named Bianzhou, a man of Heqing Prefecture and a monk of the Qiyun Hermitage on Mount Longhua. Seeing that I had become period-master of a lecture series so soon after leaving home, he of his own accord asked to expound the great Dharma, and he too roused his mind to reverently invite Master Liangru to the Qiyun Hermitage to lecture on the Shurangama Sutra. My Master generously consented to bestow the Dharma. After the fifteenth day of the first month I took leave of Yang Shaoxian and my other old friends. Seeing that I could not possibly be kept, they offered me travelling expenses; I declined them all, and they felt somewhat rebuffed, so I accepted a very little. When Master Liangru saw that I was indifferent to wealth and profit and had extinguished greed, he grew all the more affectionate toward me.

On the twenty-second we reached the Qiyun Hermitage. The native official of Lijiang Prefecture was of the Mu surname and a firm believer in the Three Jewels. By local rule no one was permitted to leave the territory, but when he heard that a good spiritual friend and a Dharma Master had come to Heqing Prefecture, he sent men to welcome them across the border, and so he came in person to reverently invite my Master. I attended my Master and went with him. The territory of Lijiang Prefecture ends in the east at the Jinsha River, in the west at the Black Water River, in the south it joins Jianchuan Prefecture, and in the north it borders on Tubo (Tibet). The native official’s residence is built against the snowy mountain, its silver peaks towering into the void, and green forests spread over the land. We stayed there half a month, questioning him on the Dharma as occasion offered.

On the eighteenth day of the second month we took our leave and returned to Heqing Prefecture, and on the twentieth began to lecture on the Shurangama Sutra. I had the good fortune to be assigned to the office of the rear hall (internal affairs). The Dharma Master Liaoran of Jianchuan Prefecture was chief seat; he was a monk of the Ten Thousand Buddhas Temple on Shishi Mountain, and in his youth had gone to the various lecture halls south of the Yangtze to study. In this lecture period, the four heads of the hall took turns to re-lecture. When Dharma Master Liaoran came to re-lecture on the chapter of the Eight Returns, he went beyond the meaning of the original sutra and overturned and belittled the chief lecturer, Master Liangru, and the assembly would not accept it. The words of Yiyun, the head of the western hall, stirred me to a moment’s impulse, and there in the lecture hall before everyone I exposed the fault of the chief seat Liaoran and imposed the penalty of the discipline board upon him. When Master Liangru learned of it he came down into the hall and asked the reason. The assembly said: ‘The chief seat has deceived his conscience, and the rear hall is upright by nature; neither of them reported to the Master. We beg the Master in his compassion to pardon them.’ Master Liang said to the chief seat: ‘In the chapter of the Eight Returns the words and the principle are plainly clear; it is you who have slandered the Dharma and brought the assembly’s anger upon yourself. You should see this clearly for yourself.’ Then he said to me: ‘You did not obey your Master’s command but used the discipline board on your own authority, and you should be heavily punished. Now, in accordance with the assembly’s judgment, I punish you lightly: kneel in penance for the burning of one stick of incense.’ Then he said to the assembly: ‘The rear hall Shaoru earnestly guards the Dharma and so steps forward to lead the assembly; he knows only that the rule may be applied, and does not know that human feeling may need to be spared.’

One day two or three who had newly left home came to the hermitage to hear the sutra, with an altogether worldly manner that was disgusting to behold. Master Liangru admonished them, saying: ‘One who leaves home must first receive the sramanera precepts. Then he receives the bhikshu precepts, and in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down he should possess the various dignities of deportment; only then can he be called a monk. If he has not received the bhikshu precepts and his deportment is incomplete, he cannot be called a monk, and he defiles the fair name of the Dharma gate.’ I was at that time in attendance beside Master Liangru, and when I heard this I bowed to the Master and said: ‘I beg the Master to transmit the bhikshu precepts to me, that I may become a proper monk.’ The Master said: ‘I am a Dharma Master. To receive the bhikshu precepts one must request a Vinaya Master.’ I asked again: ‘Who is a Vinaya Master?’ The Master said: ‘The Vinaya school is now near to being lost. In Nanjing there was the Vinaya Master Guxin, who restored the Vinaya school and is revered as its patriarch; he has already entered nirvāṇa. Among his dharma heirs, only the monk Sanmei is vigorously spreading the Vinaya, and he is now south of the Yangtze.’ I said: ‘I will go south of the Yangtze, receive the precepts, and then come back to attend upon my Master.’ The Master said: ‘It is ten thousand li and more — you speak as if it were a trifle!’ I said: ‘You yourself have said, Master, that one who has not received the bhikshu precepts cannot be called a monk. I left the Daoist gate and took refuge in the Buddha’s teaching for the sake of becoming a monk. If I cannot become a monk, what meaning is there in having shaved my head!’ The Master was silent, and I withdrew.

And so I petitioned my Master again and again, and each time my Master said not a word. On the eighth day of the fourth month the lecture period came to an end, and in the afternoon I went to the abbot’s quarters to take my leave of the Master. Seeing that my aspiration was urgent and my resolve firm, the Master said: ‘This is what your karma draws you to. Whatever lies ahead — if it is fortune, you must go and bear it; if it is hardship, you must go and bear it. Go, then!’ At that time several other men also wished to go with me, and they too asked the Master’s leave. The Master said: ‘Today, at the very start of your pilgrimage, you already have many following you. If you study well hereafter, you will become a good spiritual friend; if not, you will become a ringleader among the men of the rivers and lakes.’ I bowed in thanks and said: ‘With your compassionate prediction, Master, I shall go now and learn to be a good spiritual friend.’

In the sixth year of Chongzhen I was thirty-two. At the hour of Shen on the eighth day of the fourth month I took leave of the Qiyun Hermitage, walked twenty-five li, and begged a night’s lodging at a small hermitage. Chengzhuo had gone up Mount Jizu in the middle of the second month, and we had agreed to meet at the Three Pagodas Temple in Dali Prefecture on the twentieth day of the fourth month. I arrived at the Three Pagodas Temple on time but did not see Chengzhuo. The next day I went to the Gantong Temple to share in the merit, and only then did Chengzhuo arrive. From that time on the two of us travelled south together and never parted. After four days we came to the Gunniao Temple in the valley of the northern cliffs, where we met an acquaintance from my lay days who had left home at that temple and was serving tea to travellers. He was astonished to see me and said: ‘So you have left home and gone on pilgrimage! I grieve that I am already old and cannot go with you!’ I urged him to devote himself to the pure karma, and he made a vow to recite the Buddha-name all his life. We stayed there ten days, then took our leave and set out on the road.

On the second day of the fifth month, gazing at the white clouds, my native place lay already before my eyes, and I begged lodging at the Jinshan Temple ten li from the city. I thought of how I had been unable to support my parents in their old age, and could not bury my uncle with my own hands, and all night long my tears of rain would not dry. I thought again of my two young brothers, cast off and left behind these seven years, and how I did not know to what depths of bitterness they had fallen or whose house they now depended on. This parting of mine, this long journey — I did not know what the future held. I could not go without seeing them once. At daybreak I told Chengzhuo what was in my heart, and went out of the door; after a few steps I stopped again, turning it over and over in my mind, sighing in sorrow without end. I thought: if even now I let the affection of brothers pull at me, then at one meeting I would surely fall into the net of karma, and not only would leaving home, receiving the precepts, and cultivating fail, but there would hereafter be no way at all to repay the deep kindness of my parents and my uncle in raising me. One should see that each person has his own fixed karma and his own conditions. For all who live in this world, poverty and wealth, suffering and joy, long life and short, are what their own deeds in former lives have brought about; in this life each receives his own retribution, and even between father and son, the nearest of kin, none can take another’s place. To regret only that I cannot go and see them once — that would be to forget righteousness and benevolence and to lack compassion. Now, since there is no other way, there is only this: to turn the merit of my own cultivation over to them and to rescue them thereby! So I dried my tears and went around the city, and facing from afar the ancestral graves on the western mountain I bowed to the ground and touched my head to the earth. My heart ached as if wrung, my tears fell like rain, my two legs had no strength and I could hardly lift a step; yet I forced myself on, and reaching Guangtong County I put up for one night at an old temple.

The next day, on the road to Lufeng County, I met a relative named Zhou Zhibin, who was returning from the provincial capital to Chuxiong. He saw me from far off and called out at the top of his voice: ‘Xu Chongxiao, where are you these days? When did you leave home? Where are you going?’ I answered: ‘I left home on Mount Jizu, and now I am going south of the Yangtze to receive the precepts and study.’ He asked: ‘Have you any letter to send back?’ I said: ‘A letter could hardly make things clear. I have only two young brothers; I beg you to look after them all the more.’ As I answered, my feet did not stop. He wanted to ask more, but my heart was in grief and my throat choked so that I could not speak, and he stood by the roadside and watched me until I was far off before turning back. Chengzhuo said: ‘Since you will not go back to see them, you should at least send back a word or two.’ I said: ‘The affection of brothers must be severed and severed at once; if I send word instead, it will only stir up feelings that are hard to cut. The ancients said: “When the mind is iron and stone, the vow is firm; while love and affection are unforgotten, the supreme Way is hard to attain.”’

After several more days the provincial capital came into view, and we passed through the Biji Pass. The peaks of this pass are fair and towering, the chief of all the mountains round about; looking down on Lake Dian, it is one expanse of blue for ten thousand qing. We took a boat across Lake Dian and, landing, came to the provincial capital and lodged at the Maitreya Temple outside the city. Several friends travelling with us wished to go and look around the various temples and planned to rest here for a few days. Fearing that I might meet kin or old friends and be held back, I set out early the next morning for Songhua Dam, left by the Jinma Pass, and reached Banqiao Post-Station, where I passed one night. Chengzhuo’s lay home was in Xundian Prefecture, and he had left home at the Guanyin Hermitage in Nayi Village of Yanglin. Since it lay on our way and was not far, he invited his friends to go together with him to visit his teacher before travelling further. We crossed the Tu’er Pass and passed the night at the Heyou Hermitage, reaching there the next morning. His teacher was a man of generous character and his elder brother a plain and honest man, both cultivators of the Way. At the sight of us they welcomed us joyfully and entertained and pressed us to stay half a month; only then did we take our leave.

After walking for several days we reached Qujing Prefecture and came to Poshan, the very place where Zhuge Wuhou of old made his covenant of alliance with Meng Huo. There was an ancient temple here, and we put up for the night. I said to my companions: “This long journey of ours is not that of ordinary wandering monks. We must not simply go about admiring the scenery and neglecting true cultivation. We should buy a Luohan lamp here — a lamp above, with a reservoir of oil below — carrying it by day and using it for light by night. Each evening we take turns standing watch. After supper, at the hour of Xu, we light the lamp and sit gathered about it, each following the scripture he has studied, either reading the text or savoring its meaning, until midnight when we end the sitting. Let this be the established rule of our pilgrimage.” Everyone agreed to follow it.

We came to Pingyi Guard, passed out of the southern Yunnan border, and now touched the frontier of Guizhou. Going through Yizikong, we entered Puan Prefecture. After several more days we crossed Guansuo Ridge. This ridge is extremely lofty, a hundred li or more in circuit, and on its summit stands a military camp and a temple to Guansuo. A few days later we crossed the Pan River, where the mountain paths wind in curves, rising and falling steeply and dangerously. Within a moment a great rain poured down; the mountain streams and brooks became mountain torrents roaring like thunder, the winding paths all turned into watercourses, and a fierce wind blew in from all sides, forming whirlpools, so that one could hardly stand alone. The rain poured down from head and neck in great scoops, filling our clothes and trousers, cold to the very bone; we set our feet wide apart and moved as if riding a float-skin. When we loosened our belts to drain the water it gushed out like opening a sluice gate, and this happened several times. I said to the others: “The ancients who went seeking Dharma cast aside their very lives and did not think it hardship. Do not let this great rain make you retreat from your resolve to seek the Way; then in the future you will be able to boast to others how heroic our pilgrimage was!” Hearing this, everyone laughed, and we helped one another along, leaning on one another for support. Toward evening we reached the foot of the mountain and lodged at the Great Vow Temple. There we met a monk who had come from south of the Yangtze, and we asked him about the road ahead. He said: “These days pilgrimage is hardest of all. Everywhere there are gangs of the rivers and lakes, most of them doing the work of Mara. If they see a monk wearing a patchwork robe and sitting on a rush cushion they will not harm him; otherwise I fear your study and pilgrimage will meet with obstacles. I advise you, my friends, if you wish to have a peaceful and quiet journey, you had best exchange your baggage.” We rested ten days, then crossed the iron-chain bridge over the Pan River, where the cliffs are steep, the woods and bamboo thick and verdant, and the surging river dashes on like an arrow. This is indeed the vital passage linking Yunnan and Guizhou.

The next day we took the mountain path leading to Anzhuang Guard. The sand and stones were rough and uneven, the ridge winding and tortuous, and before long the soles of our shoes were worn through, flapping so that they could hardly be worn; we threw them away and walked barefoot. After several tens of li, we rested when night fell, and our feet were so swollen that the ankles were gone, hurting as if burned with fire and pierced with awls. In the middle of the night I thought: I have not a penny on me, and this is a solitary hermitage on a wild path where there is nowhere to beg. I should not linger here; I must set out at dawn. Then I thought again: worldly people, seeking fame and rank, wealth and honor, must still endure much hardship before they attain their wish. Today we have left home to cultivate and seek liberation from the cycle of birth and death — how can we retreat from the vow we first made just because we lack a pair of shoes! The next day I still gritted my teeth and pressed on. At first my heels hurt so much that I could not set them to the ground, and I crept along leaning on a staff; but after walking on five or six li, I could no longer feel that I had feet, and no longer felt the pain. There was no resting place along the way, and by evening I had covered more than fifty li, lodging for the night in a hermitage at Anzhuang Guard. The next day I begged a pair of straw sandals, and when I tried them on, my skin broke and blisters formed, but I paid no attention. A man of the rivers and lakes followed us for several days, and even when we rested for the night he did not leave. The next afternoon we came to a small stream crossed by a single log bridge over two zhang long. Chengzhuo and the others crossed first, and I walked slowly behind, the man trailing after me. Just as I reached the middle of the bridge, I suddenly let out a great shout, and he was so startled that he fell into the water. Pointing at him, I said: “From now on you should wash your heart and reform, and be a good man.” His face reddened to the ears, he climbed up the bank, hung his head, and took another road away.

Amid the manifold hardships we met on the road, none of my companions found them to be afflictions. Summer passed and autumn came, and in early October we at last reached Wugang Prefecture in Huguang, lodging at the Zhishui (Still Water) Hermitage. The abbot was named Yihui, a man of deep spiritual resolve; learning that we had come a long way from Yunnan, he kept us there for the winter. One day he invited me into his room for tea. I saw on the table a copy of the “Understanding of the Dharma Flower”, which I had once heard my teacher praise back in Yunnan, so it remained in my memory, and I wished to borrow it to copy, but I had no paper or brush. The abbot’s junior dharma-brother, whose Dharma name was Zhongli, was very studious, and seeing what I intended, he supplied everything I needed. That winter it snowed without cease every day, and the room was bare and open, the north wind whistling in. I wore only a single patchwork robe, and sat on the plank bed of the lodging monks with my head drawn in, copying the book; though my fingers were frozen stiff and chapped, and the ink and brush froze, I did not pause for a moment. The two dharma-brothers, seeing my firm resolve and diligence, grew all the more affectionate and respectful toward me, and gave me a padded jacket, which I received with shame — it was the first time in my life I had worn cotton clothing. Two or three of my companions took leave of us to go on pilgrimage to the sea. Chengzhuo and Juexin stayed with me.

This Wugang Prefecture lay within the fief of the princely clan of Min. There was a member of the Min clan named Yanli, fond of studying calligraphy and painting, who was acquainted with Master Yihui. In mid-October he came through the snow to the hermitage, bringing a large sheet of paper which he pasted on the wall, intending to paint a picture of “A lone fisherman in a straw cloak on a solitary boat, fishing the cold river snow”. He roughed it in with charcoal several times but still could not make up his mind. Standing by watching, I said: “In all painting, the idea must come before the brush; only when the brush is set down without further thought or hesitation can one convey its spirit. To deliberate back and forth like this, I fear, loses the natural wonder.” He turned his head to look at me and said: “Surely speaking is easy; doing it is really hard. Can you do it?” I smiled and said: “I know a little.” He handed me the brush and said: “Please paint!” I took the brush in hand, first composed the picture in my mind, then in one sweeping motion completed it, and set the brush on the table. He praised it deeply and said to Master Yihui: “Among those who have left home, there are by no means few hidden masters! Just hang this painting in the hermitage!” From then on he often came and sat with me in talk. He wrote out three scrolls in his own hand and gave them to me, Chengzhuo, and Juexin, recounting the story of his calling upon master painters everywhere.

On the fifth day of the first month, Master Heyi began to lecture on the Surangama Sutra at the Liang Family Hermitage, sixty li from the Zhishui Hermitage. Master Zhongli came to invite us along. Chengzhuo had never read the Surangama Sutra, and so set out first for the Wutai Hermitage in Baoqing Prefecture to pay a visit to Master Zhuan (
zhuān

) Yu; when the lectures were finished, he would come to the Liang Family Hermitage to join us. The three of us — myself, Master Zhongli, and Juexin — came to the Liang Family Hermitage. There were only a little over twenty in the audience, and each contributed one dan of rice and one tael of silver to form a fellowship (a joint share-out). Master Zhongli paid his contribution in full, but Juexin and I had only the patchwork robes on our backs and our rush cushions, with no money or rice to offer, and had meant merely to join in for the joy of it and leave. Master Zhongli then informed the lecturer of this, and the Master, knowing we came from the poor southern border of Yunnan, excused us from the rice and silver and graciously allowed us to attend the lectures with the assembly. I said to Juexin: “The Dharma is bestowed by the lecturer, but the food is provided by everyone’s contribution; we cannot receive it for nothing.” Thereupon the two of us volunteered for the miscellanies, washing the bowls and chopsticks, sweeping the floor and carrying water, without waiting to be called, doing whatever work there was. On the first day of the fourth month the lecture period came to a close. Zhongli stayed on, while Juexin and I took our leave and went to Baoqing Prefecture, lodging at the Great Requital of Kindness Temple.

I heard that in this temple there was a Master Ziru, a native of Yunnan, and went to pay respects to him, telling him the whole story of my leaving home and coming south. Master Ziru then addressed me as his junior dharma-brother. I asked him why he addressed me so, and he said: “I am a man of Jianchuan Prefecture, and left home to become a monk at Shishi Mountain. In my youth I studied the scriptures under the old Master Liangru, and relied upon that venerable elder for six years, deeply taking in his Buddhist teachings. To this day we have had no news of each other. Now that I see Master Shaoru, it is as if I see the venerable teacher himself. So if we speak of our Dharma lineage, I should call you my junior dharma-brother. In Yunnan, what scripture did you hear your teacher lecture on?” I answered: “I once heard the Dharma Flower and the Surangama, but only planted the seed of it; I did not grasp its meaning.” He asked again: “Where have you come from today?” I answered: “From the Liang Family Hermitage in Wugang Prefecture, and I only came here after hearing Master Heyi lecture on the Surangama.” Master Ziru said: “Master Heyi is my fellow cultivator and friend. You have arrived at just the right moment this time. Master Zhuan Yu has just brought out a new work, the Commentary on the Four Meanings of the Surangama, and the lay supporters who protect the Dharma have asked to have it printed and circulated. The Master has ordered me to expound it in this temple in his place; the audience already numbers over a hundred. There is just a vacancy for the post of managing the back hall — you may take on this office.” I said: “It is enough to give me a scattered place to lodge; the post of head of the seats I would not dare to accept.” Master Ziru said: “A lion’s cub has no need for such excessive modesty. I will provide you with monk’s robes and shoes and socks, and you may enter the hall and take up the duties.” I said: “I beg you to grant me two things: first, let me still enter the hall and sit and sleep with my patchwork robe and rush cushion; and second, I beg the abbot not to have someone offer me extra meals. If only I may hear the scriptures and taste the flavor of the Dharma, I shall be overflowing with gratitude and nothing more.” But Master Ziru disagreed and insisted that I change into new clothes. At the time there was a resident monk of the temple named Yexi, also among the audience, who had long followed Master Zhuan Yu.

The next day he went to the Wutai Hermitage to pay respects to the Master, and when the Master asked about the affairs of the lecture period, he reported my background and my entreaties to the Master. The Master said: “When I was young, at the Bamboo Grove Temple on the Northern Five Terraces, I relied upon Master Yuechuan and attended the lectures with the assembly; I too wore a patchwork robe and straw sandals, with a staff, a bamboo hat, and a rush cushion. Later I began to wander, to the Tiantai and the Southern Peak and other places, and onward to this Baoqing, and I was still the same, never changing. Because these lay patrons built this hermitage, and knelt on the ground holding clothes and shoes with both hands begging me to change, and would not rise if I refused, I followed their wish, also in order to give rise to their faith. I have often seen meditation monks unwilling to change this habit; they all love it, and it is rare to see one willing to walk a different path. Today to hear that this monk from Yunnan is not turned by circumstances — he truly resembles my own conduct in former days. Go back and tell Master Ziru to follow his original resolve and not to force him! In doing this one can instruct the assembly not to be greedy.” Master Ziru then granted me what I wished. Among the assembly there were some who praised my simplicity, and some who mocked me for seeking to be different; but to these praises and gibes alike I turned a deaf ear.

Three days after the lecture period began, the abbot ordered the four heads of the seats to lecture in turn, each to speak six times. The head of the western hall having gone out on business, and the prior pleading illness, only the chief of the hall, Master Kedu, remained — a dharma-heir of Master Wuxue of Jingci Peak on the Southern Peak, by nature simple, sincere, and fond of study, who shared my aspirations and with whom I felt a mutual respect. From the fourth fascicle of the Commentary on the Four Meanings of the Surangama onward, the two of us took turns expounding it to the very end. When the Dharma assembly came to a close, Master Ziru led the company to the Wutai Hermitage to thank Master Zhuan Yu. The Master happened to be seated cross-legged beneath an umbrella, whence his style “the Umbrella-Dwelling Daoist”. After Master Ziru had paid his respects, he returned to the Great Requital of Kindness Temple. The Master detained me, and gave me a meal beneath the umbrella; the one dish was a plate of bitter melon. The Master first took a bite with his chopsticks, and at the same time bade me eat. I put a piece in my mouth; it was bitter and hard to swallow, yet I dared not spit it out. Seeing this, the Master laughed and said to me: “First bitter, then sweet — so it is for one who cultivates the Way and becomes a good spiritual friend.” I bowed in thanks for his instruction. The Master said: “You have a little strength of bone. Where do you plan to go afterward?” I said: “When I set out from Yunnan, I was seeking Master Sanmei in order to receive the precepts, and after that to study as I pleased.” The Master said: “Master Sanmei is a true Vinaya master; you may go to him to receive the precepts. But as for ‘studying as you please’ — in the monasteries of the south, most lecture halls do not keep strict rules, and many people are arrogant and reckless. If you find it not to your liking, come back to me here; above all, do not drift along with the current and indulge yourself outside. In the future you will certainly be a pillar of the Dharma.” He then had his attendant bring a set of the works he had himself written and gave them to me, and once more enjoined and encouraged me, saying: “Learn my conduct and my practice.” I bowed, received them, and took my leave.

The next day I asked Chengzhuo to go with me on pilgrimage to the Southern Peak. Setting out from Baoqing Prefecture, we walked for five days, passed Yangliu Pool, climbed up over the back mountain, and roamed the Nine Dragon Flat and the Ancient Great Flat, on the side of which was a pool called the Pheasant Pool. When Master Sanmei came to this pool, a dragon had transformed into a pheasant and beat its wings up from the heart of the water, and Master Sanmei gave it the three refuges and five precepts. We also paid respects at Maoping and other temples, and rounding the Heavenly Pillar Peak and the Misty Cloud Peak, went down from the Zhurong Peak to the front of the Southern Peak Temple, where we lodged at the Tea-Bestowing Hermitage. There we met a wandering cloud-water monk and asked him about the road ahead. He said: “Now the bandits are raging, sweeping on through Changde, Tanzhou, Gongan, Jingzhou, and other places. The defenses everywhere are strict. The officers and soldiers are no better; they often seize the monks’ baggage and then falsely accuse them of being spies and arrest them, so that one has no place to lodge a grievance and suffers every misery. You masters must on no account go down the mountain!” Hearing this, Chengzhuo and I were not frightened in our hearts; I thought, could we have walked thousands of li on foot and come to naught! So we asked the abbot whether any other road led through. He said: “The world is in such chaos; it would be best to stay on here for a while and set out when all is peaceful. There is no need to be impatient!” I said: “My resolve is fixed, and time waits for no one! I beg you to point out another road, and I shall be very grateful.” He said: “There is indeed another road, but it is very desolate and few travel it, all of it mountains and deep ravines. You must go by way of Qianyang to Huitong, then to Lülin County, and past the Puan Cihua Temple; when you reach there, ask the way to Wanzai County, then to Ruizhou Prefecture, and you can reach the provincial city of Jiangxi. This road avoids the places where the wandering bandits are making havoc.” The next morning we set out along the route he had told us. Sure enough, ridge after ridge of mountains, no village in sight, utterly desolate; sometimes we went from morning meal straight on until evening, sometimes setting out without any breakfast at all. Every day we covered no less than seventy or eighty li. Only after half a month did we come round to the provincial city of Jiangxi, and lodged at the Tower Under the Pagoda Temple. After resting three days we went through Dean County, roamed Mount Lu, and paid respects at the Guizong, Kaixi, and Wuru temples.

One day we came to the Wansong (Ten Thousand Pines) Hermitage. As the sky was darkening we knocked on the door to ask lodging, but the monk of the hermitage glared at us in anger and shut the door with a slam, refusing us. By now it was quite dark, and the bright stars were shining. With no help for it, we had to find some place to stay the night. We saw a great rock jutting out over the side of the road, with a space of over a zhang underneath. We three squeezed in, set down our rush cushions, and sat waiting for dawn. After a while the gate of the temple opened again, and that monk came to drive us away once more. The three of us sighed that our conditions did not match, yet rather pitied the man for his folly; we paid him no heed, and sat on through the night by force of will. When the east was about to lighten, the three rose and went along the road. We came to Douyeping, ate a morning meal, and went on to roam the Drying Grain Stone and the Looking-Up-to-Sky Flat, and even wandered the Golden Bamboo Flat. As the sun was about to set in the west we came to the Donglin Temple and lodged there. The meditation hall of the temple was in the back. The cloud-water hall had only three rooms, utterly desolate: wild grass covering the ground a foot or more high, walls fallen and tiles gone, doors and windows without any covering. In the temple there was a Beamed Hall. We went in to pay respects to the Buddha, and found the dust thickly gathered and the filth of pigeons and sparrows everywhere. Chengzhuo and I swept the Buddha hall clean and set our rush cushions to the left of the Buddha image, planning to sit in Buddha-recitation through the whole night, that we might not have come in vain to this ancient White Lotus Society. But the monk in charge came out from within, reproached us for not first telling the officers before lodging privately in the great hall, and with a loud voice abused us and drove us out, all the way to the mountain gate. An old monk who lived there as a sponsor of the temple asked us to stay to eat, and let us lodge. Then the monk in charge came again to reproach the old monk, and even splashed water on the ground so that we could not sit or lie. Taking leave of the old monk, the three of us went out of the mountain gate.

I said to Chengzhuo and Juexin: across many lives and births we must have planted karmic conditions displeasing to that monk in charge, and today we are receiving the retribution. Think of him as a good spiritual friend, helping us accomplish the practice of patience and forbearance; we must by no means give rise to a mind of resentment. But still we could find no place to lodge. Chengzhuo said: “When we were coming up just now, I saw a dense grove of trees on the road below; we can go there to pass the night.” We went down and sought the grove, but it proved to be an old grave. The three of us set down our rush cushions and sat on the ground. The open country stretched empty and still, without a sound; there was no moonlight, and it was pitch dark, so that we could not see our own fingers. When we had sat until the first watch of the night, we suddenly heard a cry: “Catch him!” and all around, voices shouting in unison: “Catch the thief!” I said to Chengzhuo and Juexin: “If he should chase us here in earnest, black and white confounded and no way to speak in our defense, then it will be our fixed karma.”

When dawn came, we heard in the distance the bells of post horses, and only then knew that the road outside was a highway; our hearts were a little at ease. The three of us came out of the grove and saw a man working in the fields. We went up and asked him why the shouting had risen in unison all around the night before. He said: “The wheat in the fields is ripe now, and we were guarding against thieves; that is why we all shouted together — merely to frighten off robbers.” At this the three of us burst out laughing.

We went at once to the Xilin Temple to pay respects, and passed the night there. The next day we reached Jiujiang Prefecture, when the sun had already sunk west. Every hermitage outside the city refused to take us in, saying the local authorities strictly forbade harboring outsiders, and told us to go across the river where there would be lodging. We had no choice but to cross the river on an empty stomach. When the boat reached midstream the ferryman demanded his fare, and I untied the cloth I used to bind my legs and gave it to him. Among those on the boat was a Daoist who, seeing the state we were in, paid our fare for us. After we landed, we asked someone nearby whether there was any place to lodge in the vicinity. He answered that there was no monastery close by, but if we went seventy li down the river embankment to Zaogang, there was a place called the Five Patriarchs’ Mother-Separation Mound, where there was a tea hermitage that received monks. I said to Chengzhuo and Juexin: “We have been deceived. The tea hermitage ahead is still far, and the southwest wind is blowing hard; we had best hurry as fast as we can and not hesitate here.” The three of us braved the fierce wind, muffling mouth and face, and hurried along beneath the moon, reaching the place only in the small hours. We knocked on the door and begged lodging, and it was fortunate that the abbot, a man of compassion in spirit, rose at once and opened the door and bade us enter, asking why we were traveling so late at night. We told him all in detail. He gave a long sigh, felt the hardship of pilgrimage, and gladly prepared tea for us. I said in praise: if not for the hermitage at Jiujiang, how would this man’s depth of spirit be shown!

After breakfast the next day we asked him about the road ahead, and learned that the various patriarch-temples along the way had all fallen into ruin, and only by good fortune had the old Master Sanmei had them repaired (
qì

) and restored. We resolved to go and reverently visit them. We set out for Huangmei County, climbed Mount Poe, and paid respects at the sanctuary of the Fourth Patriarch; then on to Fengmao Mountain, the sanctuary of the Fifth Patriarch; up the High Mountain Temple to the sanctuary of Master Jingjian; over the Bell Ridge to the Old Temple, the sanctuary of the Thousand-Year-Old Caudex Master Baozhang; on to Qianshan County, the sanctuary of the Third Patriarch; and to Qingyang County, to worship at Mount Jiuhua. Looking down from the great hall we saw a hermitage and went to lodge for the night, but it provided no evening meal. The next morning we sat a long while waiting for breakfast, when we saw the abbot come to tell us: “The hermitage is poor and has no means; I can only give you an empty place, not provide meals. To eat you may go to the room-chiefs and beg a meal.” I said to my two companions: “The room-chief’s kitchen is a meat kitchen; where would there be pure food there? Let us go elsewhere!” Thereupon we went up to the hall and bowed before the Bodhisattva, and went down the mountain with empty stomachs. After walking more than ten li we came to a lodging hermitage and only then ate a little.

We arrived at Taiping Prefecture and heard that Master Rongwu was lecturing on the Dharma Flower Sutra at the Qingshan Temple, not far from the prefectural city. We gladly asked the way and went, reaching the temple just as the sun had set. Seeing that we all carried staffs, hats, and rush cushions, the monk in charge would not give us lodging. When we begged him again and again, he saw the day was far spent and hard to travel, and had someone lead us out of the mountain gate to a small local-earth-god shrine by the road to lodge. The three of us stacked our rush cushions and sat facing one another. I said: “Since we have come in quest of the Dharma, how can we return empty-handed!” Early the next morning we walked back to the temple, ate the morning gruel, sat through one session of the lecture, and then went down the mountain, begging food and asking the way of the villagers, and went on our way. At about the hour of Si on the tenth day, we reached Nanjing. From afar we saw the jeweled pagoda of the Bao’en Temple, its five colors soaring into the sky, gleaming in the sun. We went in, bowed, and circled the pagoda. By noon we were hungry with nothing to eat, and asked one of those who were circumambulating where there was a hall that received monks. Someone pointed to the Tripitaka Hall in the southern corridor and said: “There it is.” We went there, bowed to the Buddha, sat beside the steps of the hall, and saw monks coming and going, yet no one came forward to greet us. The three of us did not know the reason, so we rose and went out, where we met an old monk and asked him the cause. He said: “Nanjing is a place of lecture halls and meditation halls. If your clothes and shoes are neat and proper, you are a meditation guest, and someone receives you. You are wandering monks on pilgrimage, and so no one concerns themselves with you.”

We then entered the city and lodged at the Great Buddha Hermitage, west of the bell and drum tower. There was no great hall there, only a mat canopy of reeds spread over the Buddha image. The abbot was a man of genuine practice, receiving the assembly with a bowl of rice and delighted to see us. Knowing we came from Yunnan, he said: “The abbot of the Xingshan Temple here, whose Dharma name is Yinwu, is a landsman of yours. You may go there, and he will certainly take you in.” At noon the next day we reached there and were given lodging. We saw that the great assembly all ate rice from weevil-ridded, long-stored grain, and the vegetable was only ill-salted, stinking pickles of the meanest sort. When we went into the guest quarters to have a look about, we saw that the resident monks of the temple themselves ate fresh seasonal vegetables and clean white rice. The abbot’s disciple, named Kuoran, was also a man of Yunnan, and recognized our accent. That night he came to the cloud-water hall to claim kinship, and I said we were men of Guizhou. He asked again, seeming as though he wished to keep us. I said to Chengzhuo and Juexin: “We have come over ten thousand li and should rely upon a good spiritual friend of virtue. Toward a man like this, who does not consider others, we would rather willingly accept hardship and privation than go near him.”

Hearing that Master Juewu was lecturing on the Surangama Sutra at the Yuanjue Hermitage, we went out of the city to listen. It happened that some good supporters were making a charitable offering of food to the monks. All monks from the ten directions who came sat on the floor of the Skanda Hall, with a dish of four kinds of vegetables for every two people. I happened to share a meal with a wandering monk. I myself was attentive to my deportment and ate slowly; but he never let his chopsticks pause, and in one breath finished off all four dishes. When the meal was done and we had gone out, I said to my two friends: “In the future, if we have the conditions to set out a meal for the assembly, let the vegetables be served in large bowls no matter how many kinds, and let everyone eat freely. In this way, on the one hand we can make everyone pay attention to a monk’s deportment, and on the other we can give rise to the assembly’s faith and reverence. A man like the one today has utterly lost the character of a monk — how is he different from a starving fellow!”

We went again to the Pude Temple to pay respects and wander about, and entered the meditation hall for lodging. That night we discussed the matter, saying: now the tenth month is nearly past, and it is too cold for traveling on the road. It would be better to stay here a while and set out again in the warm spring. After the gruel the next morning we asked the temple controller for a lodging-place, and he said: “I cannot give lodging even to two of you, let alone three.” Then he looked at me and said: “As for the lamp-attendant’s place in the bell-and-board hall, I can give it to you alone.” I said with a smile: “I am a clumsy fellow with rough hands and clumsy feet, and cannot trim the glazed lamps.” The three of us packed our things and went out of the mountain gate. I said to Chengzhuo and Juexin: “Since the monasteries of the capital will give none of the three of us lodging, let us for the time being scatter and pass the winter separately, and agree to meet on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month. I hear that Baohua Mountain sets great store by studying the scriptures; I want to go there to study the Surangama Dharani.” Chengzhuo said: “Juexin and I will go to the Ancestral Hall; come over when you have finished studying the mantra.” I exchanged my rush cushion for a sleeping-mat with Juexin, and the three of us parted ways.

When I had climbed a little way up the slope of Baohua Mountain the sun had set, and I lodged at the Shimen (Stone Gate) Hermitage. At tea that evening I asked the abbot of the hermitage: “I hear Baohua set great store by the study of scriptures, and I wish to go.” The host said: “In the mountain there is an old head instructor, a man of Yunnan, who long dwelt in the northern capital. He has been on Baohua Mountain ten years and has read the great canon three times, and he delights most in those who study diligently. I too once studied scriptures under him. There are few people in the temple; there are four room-chiefs, and by good fortune everyone eats from a single pot, so no separate meals are made. Although all three meals are but thin gruel, the wandering cloud-water monks who come and go to worship the copper hall are all given lodging and food. Since you wish to stay on the mountain to study, you must set body and mind down and not mind the poverty and meagerness there.” The next morning I climbed the mountain, and reaching the resident temple, bowed to the Buddha, and then went about wandering here and there and paid respects to the resident monks for a whole day. In a subtle way I felt the place was familiar, as if I had been here before. I paid respects to the head instructor, bowed, and told him I wished to study the Surangama Dharani. The Master asked: “What place are you from? How many years have you been a monk? This mantra should be read through in advance until you know it well.” I said I was a man of Yunnan, had just left home to come south, and was illiterate, so I had not read it. Thereupon the Master consented, saying: “Since you have come to the mountain, you may work at the hall (washing bowls and delivering meals and the like), and lodge in the kitchen.”

When the eleventh month came, the weather was freezing. The washed bowls, stacked together, froze into a single mass and were hard to separate; so each time after washing them I dried them with a clean cloth, and the next morning when I used them they separated easily. For the water-drawer one man could not keep up the supply, and I helped carry water as well. The monk in charge of the kitchen, whose Dharma name was Liaoran, was young and quick. There were also room-chiefs (monks in charge of the storerooms) who each day measured out the rice and vegetables and handed them to the kitchen monk to cook into a meal or a soup. But once things passed through that kitchen monk’s hands, he would hold back a portion for himself. One day, when I came back from reciting the Surangama Dharani, he had kept back some rice and asked me to eat. I asked him: “The assembly eats gruel; where does this rice come from?” He said: “I keep it back for you out of good will, and you still question me!” I said: “A great man — how can he eat food of unknown origin!” And I rose and left. From then on the kitchen people banded together, shielding one another, and found it hard to let me live with them. That kitchen monk privately discussed with the controller that, since no one was in the board hall (the hall in the temple that kept the watch), I should be made to keep watch there, tending the incense and striking the board (in old times time was kept by the burning of incense, and at the appointed hour the board was struck as a signal). This hall was bare and open, with a wide monk’s bed; I slept there alone, as if in an ice cave. There was an old room-chief, a eunuch who had left home, who had the most compassionate heart of all, and pitying me for my high resolve in poverty, one dark night pushed open the door and came in, and whispered close to my ear: “Take this thing to ward off the cold!” Then he went out again.
