They came to nine hundred and seventy-six taels and five mace of silver, which I handed over to the Steward, Master Dazhao, in the presence of the assembly. That night I remembered that when the temple’s orientation was first changed, the Monk had instructed Master Dazhao, saying: ‘My relic pagoda may hereafter be built behind the great hall.’ And I had often observed that among the monasteries everywhere, wherever a pagoda stands behind the main hall, the place does not prosper. The Monk ought to be asked to fix the site of the pagoda himself. The next day I came to the abbot’s quarters and, beating about the bush, said: ‘We rejoice that the Master has consented to the building of the long-life pagoda. May we know where the Master has decided to build it?’ The Monk said: ‘Have you forgotten? I said behind the great hall.’ I said: ‘I once heard a geomancer discussing the earth-veins with the Master, and he said that there are three turnings (cycles): a great turning must rest a hundred and twenty years before it turns and prospers, a middle turning must rest eighty years before it prospers, and a small turning must rest forty years before it can prosper. Behind this great hall lies the incoming vein. If the earth-vein should turn and no longer prosper, later men will say the long-life pagoda damaged the feng shui, and the pagoda will very likely have to be moved and altered. Better to build it at the dragon’s head, to keep it secure forever. If the pagoda prospers, the monastery prospers; if the monastery prospers, the pagoda prospers.’ After a long while the Monk said: ‘Let it be as you think: build it at the dragon’s head.’ Master Dazhao and Master Huimu, the chief seat, and others were standing by at the time, and I said: ‘You elders have all heard it: the Master himself has said that the pagoda is not to be built behind the hall, but is to be built in front, at the dragon’s head.’

On the first day of the intercalary sixth month of that year the Monk told an attendant to bring the almanac, and after looking at it he said: ‘At the hour of Si on the fourth day (between nine and eleven in the morning) I shall enter nirvāṇa.’ He at once had the gavel struck (the instrument used in the temple to summon the assembly when some grave matter arises) and gathered the community in the abbot’s quarters, and said: ‘The Dharma seat of Baohua Mountain — Jianyue may succeed to it.’ He took up the purple robe and the precept volume and delivered them to me, saying: ‘I lay this matter upon you as a charge and a burden: to hold the three trainings (precepts, samadhi, and wisdom) and to make the light of the precepts shine forth.’ I knelt on the ground and reported: ‘This humble one is the last of all in precept-age and in cultivated virtue; I beg the Master to hand it to one of the Acharya Masters! This humble one is willing to assist and support him in teaching!’ The Monk at once turned his face to the wall and lay silent. Thinking to accord with the Master’s wish for the time being, I said: ‘This humble one receives the Master’s compassionate command; for the present I shall keep watch over it, and when the Master’s health is wholly restored I shall deliver it back to the abbot’s quarters.’ Only then did the Monk say with a gentle face: ‘It is not today that I first entrusted it to you; this thought has long been in my mind. You need not decline again!’ I bowed, accepted, and rose; then I said to Master Duxing: ‘Your virtue and your precept-age are both good; you should be Acharya (the master who transmits the precepts), and may serve as a model for students who come after.’ To Master Dazhao I said: ‘You shall remain prior, to assist Jianyue.’ On the fourth day the Monk gathered the assembly in the abbot’s quarters, had water brought to bathe and wash his body, and said to them all: ‘When the water on my body is dry, I shall go. Do not think of me as coming or going; you must not wear mourning or weep aloud, nor send out obituary notices in any direction. All worldly ceremonies are to be dispensed with entirely. Three days from now, bury me on Dragon Mountain behind the temple.’ Then he had them recite the Buddha’s name. When the water was dry he passed away in the cross-legged posture with a smile on his face. His body was laid in offering in the abbot’s quarters, and everything was done according to the Monk’s dying command. The assembly recited the sutras in all sincerity for three days, and then the Dharma assembly, holding incense, flowers, banners, and pennants, escorted the Monk to Dragon Mountain, where a whole-body pagoda was built and offerings made. I could not bear to go back to my cell, and wished to keep the pagoda for three years as a sweeping and tending servant, with only a reed mat over my head, regardless of wind and rain, reciting the sutras day and night to repay his deep kindness. In less than a month the assembly pressed me to return to the temple and installed me in the abbot’s quarters.

At that time Acharya Xiangxue was in Suzhou, and when he heard that the Monk had entered nirvāṇa and had transmitted the robe and bowl to me, he did not approve in his heart. He took a boat from Suzhou upstream, intending to go to the land of Chu, and passed through Longtan without even entering Baohua Mountain. Only when Master Dazhao wrote him a letter in his own hand earnestly urging him did he return to the mountain and pay homage at the Monk’s reliquary pagoda. Afterwards he engaged craftsmen to cut and print in the Great Compassion Hall the book he had himself compiled, A String of Pearls Through the Shurangama Sutra, and left the Great Compassion Hall in a shocking litter. I suggested to Master Xiang that he move the cutting to the side chamber, and Master Xiang said: ‘Today you think cutting sutras in the hall is unclean; when the future comes and the rooms stand empty, the mats bare, the dust thick and the grass deep, I fear there will be no one to help sweep it!’ I said gravely: ‘Master Xiang, mind your words. This temple is the dwelling of dragons and devas, and the radiance of our forebear; I think it will not come to such a pass! There is no need to trouble Master Xiang to fret over my future!’ With that I returned to the abbot’s quarters and turned the matter over carefully in my mind, and my lament turned to gladness. What Master Xiang said today should be taken as an added and superior condition aiding me onward (a spur driving me to advance), steadying my vow and my will, to hold up the Dharma gate. I ought as soon as possible to draw up rules and regulations, first doing away with abuses, and then conduct myself according to the proper norms.

That very night I drew up ten articles of regulation. The next day I gathered the assembly and respectfully invited the two Masters Xiangxue and Dazhao, and reported to them: ‘This humble one is poor in conduct and light in merit, yet by the Monk’s charge and burden I preside over Baohua Mountain. I have now drawn up ten articles as rules, from which no party is exempt. Therefore I have come to beg you two Masters to bear witness while I announce them to the assembly.’

1. I have often seen that in the ancient temples everywhere each branch household keeps its own stove and manages its own affairs, while the halls stand silent and deserted, and one seldom meets a monk who practises austerely, so that the monastery daily declines. The fault lies with those who presided before, who did not carefully weigh the character of those who sought the Way but shaved heads indiscriminately. Today I vow that Baohua Mountain shall prosper forever: I shall put an end to the affliction of branch households, and let only those who are kin in the Dharma, wearing the robe, live together in harmony; I swear that I will not shave and ordain a single disciple of my own.

2. I have often seen men in the monasteries hoarding wealth and piling up money for their old age, and even the young receiving offerings, living loose and unrestrained, refusing to cultivate, enjoying the fruits of others’ labour without a trace of shame. They infect one another and set the assembly at odds, so that the donors and Dharma protectors mock and ridicule them, and the temple gate loses its lustre. This custom Baohua Mountain must thoroughly abolish. Even those who cultivate in old age shall not lay up private funds, but dwell together as conditions allow.

3. In most monasteries everywhere a master of alms is appointed (a monk charged with cultivating donors abroad and soliciting money and goods for the temple), and books of karmic connection are handed out far and wide for soliciting donations. The abbot too praises this snare-like practice, and the officers run about currying favour, so that the alms-master takes the credit and cheats the assembly, and gets the stewardship into his grasp. To act thus greatly perverts cause and effect and cools the trust of the donors. Today Baohua Mountain shall appoint no alms-master and hand out no book of karmic connection. Let the provisions for the Way come of themselves; a true cultivator will certainly not go hungry.

4. In the monasteries everywhere, once a leading elder is honoured as abbot he sets up a small kitchen, gathers and stores up fruit, prepares his own food, and eats privately as he pleases. Those who find favour with the abbot may share it, but all the rest never taste a morsel. Such unequal dealing with the assembly ought to make a man ashamed of holding the empty name of one who leads the multitude. Though a seat for the abbot is provided in the refectory, he seldom appears there. Today I shall take the three daily meals of gruel and rice in the hall with the assembly, and all fruit shall go into the store. If donors and Dharma protectors come up the mountain, the courtesy between host and guest cannot be set aside; and that is not to be counted as partiality to the assembly.

5. The heads of halls everywhere each receive the offerings of donors separately. Incense offerings should be handed in to the abbot’s quarters, and the funds for a vegetarian feast should be paid into the treasury; this is what is meant by dividing the common into two. But if a donor offers only an incense gift and this is kept as private property, while entertaining guests is left for the resident community to bear, then the Steward is burdened with the care of the seven necessities (the seven daily requisites such as oil, salt, firewood, and rice). In such conduct there is no thought of the rule that “the monastery is mine, and all my possessions belong wholly to the monastery.” Today, though the conditions about me are not complete, I shall abolish this abuse beforehand. All incense offerings shall belong wholly to the monastery. Anyone who uses them privately must make the income and outlay known to the assembly.

6. Nowadays when the precepts are transmitted everywhere, notices are posted, and whether the period lasts three weeks or a month, all who come must pay a lodging fee, and when they leave, each is given a subscription list (a book for soliciting alms). To use such means to do trade is not truly to spread the Dharma. Henceforth on Baohua Mountain those who come to seek the precepts and gather together shall pay no lodging fee, nor shall a subscription list be given them when they leave; simply and plainly, as the season allows, shall the precepts be transmitted in purity.

7. In the great and famous temples everywhere, each cell privately stores tea and fruit and sets out curiosities for display. Not only do several men sit together in idle talk, wasting the hours in emptiness, but they discuss the rights and wrongs and the merits and faults of others, so that the minds of the assembly are set at variance. To do so brings much loss and little gain — how can such men digest the offerings of the faithful! Therefore today I abolish it altogether. Let all who dwell together in harmony: if a friend in the Way comes to visit, or an acquaintance comes on business, invite him to the guest cell and entertain him simply. Thus, first, the monastery does not appear lacking in courtesy to guests, and second, one’s own face gains lustre.

8. The heads of the halls in the monasteries everywhere are in the habit of offering congratulations and condolences to lay families on occasions of joy and mourning, sending money and gifts to curry favour with donors. Having left the lay household, they yet perform lay ceremonies; being monks, they do not cherish the dignity of the monk, and for the sake of gain they violate the Buddha’s rule altogether. Now Baohua Mountain lies far from the towns, and moreover the whole assembly lives according to the Buddha’s Vinaya; all donors of right faith will surely understand and look upon us with forbearance.

9. A temple set deep in the mountains differs from a monastery near the towns: firewood, rice, and the like must be carried up the mountain on one’s back. Henceforth when there is common work (labour in which all must lend a hand), the wooden clapper shall sound as the signal, and all shall turn out together to work. If a man does not move himself but orders others to labour, he cannot be said to lead the assembly. Henceforth, whenever there is work on the slopes, I shall not shrink to the rear; in every kind of labour I shall be the first to set my own hand to it. The sick shall not be pressed, and only the aged may rest. All who dwell here together shall follow this practice.

10. All who dwell within the same boundary must observe the Buddha’s rule: put aside all ornaments and beloved trifles, wear no silk, and let your clothing not be cut in the lay fashion. The three robes shall never be parted from you and must be dyed to the subdued colour; one bowl you shall always use, whether of clay or of iron. Food after midday the Vinaya nowhere permits; all must practise according to the teaching and urge one another on, and the slothful will of themselves grow diligent.
If I settle these ten matters today as rules for the assembly, why should Baohua Mountain fear that it will not prosper?

Master Dazhao said: ‘The other articles may perhaps be changed in this way, but as for the matter of the alms-master, that can by no means be dispensed with. If this is made public today, I fear the flow of grain will be cut off hereafter, and then repentance will come too late!’ I said: ‘Though this humble one has but newly taken up the abbacy, in truth I too lack the conditions. I vow never to imitate the bustle of the monasteries elsewhere, with their thresholds like a marketplace; I am resolved to follow the model of the ancients’ conduct.’ When Master Xiang heard this he said not a word, but left with his head held high. Master Da was displeased too, and went back to his cell with a sigh.

In the lifetime of the late Monk there were three eunuchs who had taken refuge with him: the eunuch Sun, whose style was Dunwu; the eunuch Liu, whose style was Dunxiu; and the eunuch Zhang, whose style was Dunzheng. When the Prince of Yu crossed the river, the three fled into the mountain and sought to leave home. The late Monk was then away and had not returned, and it was Master Dazhao who hung up the Monk’s portrait in the central hall and shaved the three of them. By the time the Monk came back to the mountain the three were already dwelling each in his own monk’s cell. On the thirtieth day of the ninth month Liu Dunxiu privately took counsel with Master Xiangxue and Master Dazhao, wishing to light a fire in his own room and set up a small kitchen. Both Masters agreed. On the first day of the tenth month he invited me to his room to drink tea, and the two Masters were already seated there. Dunxiu told me of his wish to set up a small kitchen and said that both Masters Xiang and Da had already consented, and that he was now informing the new abbot of the matter. I said: ‘Since I am the abbot, why was this not discussed together, instead of being privately agreed first and made known to me afterwards? Today I have three things to tell you. First, in the late Monk’s lifetime, whenever anyone anywhere invited him to open a precept transmission period, if there were private small stoves, pots, bowls, and the like, he always had them destroyed first, so that all might share one great kitchen, and only then would he accept the invitation and go; if they were not destroyed, he would not go. The Monk has been in nirvāṇa less than four months — who dares to set up a private small kitchen in this monastery? That is to deceive the late Master, and can by no means be done. Second, if you insist on setting up a small kitchen, then wait until I am dead, and perhaps you may do as you please. Third, if I should leave this place for other conditions and cease to be abbot of Baohua Mountain, then the Masters may decide as they wish. But while I dwell on this mountain, how could I consent to let it fall into decay and ruin!’ With that I shook out my sleeves and left the room. Masters Xiang and Da said nothing, and Dunxiu flushed red with disappointment. And from this occasion I made a beginning of restoring the precepts to vigour.

One day I gathered the assembly in the Great Hero Hall and invited the two Masters Xiangxue and Dazhao. When I had bowed, I said to the assembly: ‘In the past, when I attended upon the late Monk, I joined with the various Masters in assisting the Monk in the work of teaching and guiding. In all matters I first reported them carefully to the Masters. Now I wish to alter this. I once heard the Monk’s compassionate instruction: “From the Patriarch of the Vinaya down to me, everything was done from skilful means and expedient devices, for the sake of restoring the Vinaya. Since your aspiration is to spread the Vinaya, hereafter you shall follow the Vinaya rules and practise them in your own person.” Today this humble one bears the responsibility alone, and the responsibility is mine; I can by no means know the Vinaya and yet act contrary to it. Now that I have made this clear to the assembly, what is a rule must be obeyed, and what is a Dharma must be practised.’ Three days later Master Dazhao resigned the office of Steward; Dunwu roused his mind and took on the prior’s duties; Master Xiangxue went to Tianning Temple in Changzhou to lecture on the sutras; the various fellow ordinands each went their own way; and of the former officers of the halls, eight or nine out of ten departed. As for those who could not, first, practise the Vinaya in their own persons, second, keep the pure and simple life in common with the assembly and take delight in plain living, and third, go out to work and bear toil — I did not hold them back either. Those who remained were more than a hundred like-minded men, all resolved and diligent, helping one another, with one common vow to uphold the precepts.

In the middle of the tenth month more than thirty seekers of the precepts came, with Longsha of Yancheng County at their head. I first chanted the proclamation of the boundary and marked out the simā according to the Vinaya, and then ordained them as full bhikshus three men to a platform. Master Dazhao and the various friends in the Way said nothing to my face, but afterwards there was much talk: they said that I, who had received the late Monk’s charge, was now greatly altering the traditional ritual of ordination — that chanting the boundary and marking out the simā was rarely heard of, and three men to a platform never seen — and they accused me of the crime of unfilial conduct. It was because they were not well versed in the Vinaya that they spoke so. When I heard it I made as if I had not. One day Master Dazhao strolled into the abbot’s quarters, and I gently urged him, saying: ‘If you have leisure, pray go back and read through the Vinaya section of the canon; it will pass the time, and what do you think of it?’ He read through the Vinaya collection, and only then understood that what I had done had its grounds; in his heart he was instead filled with admiration. All the talk there had been died away of itself.

When Liu Dunxiu was still a eunuch he had given Sun Dunwu four hundred taels of silver to buy some farmland near the monastery, so that he might provide for his old age. Dunwu’s heart was not honest: he bought poor land at a high price, and the acreage fell short, and the rents and grain he collected were mostly in arrears. Liu Dunxiu therefore hated him bitterly and carried a sharp axe hidden on his person, vowing to cut Sun Dunwu down. It looked as though some dreadful deed would be done, and everyone was alarmed and frightened. Master Dazhao told me of the matter, and I said that once trouble broke out within the walls it would ruin the monastery. Fortunately there was still a surplus of the silver for building the pagoda, and I used it to buy incense for offering at the pagoda and so to reconcile the two men. Dunxiu also reduced the price by a hundred taels, and only then was the monastery quieted again.

In the spring of the third year of Shunzhi the Bannermen turned their horses out to graze, and the horses ate the people’s wheat. The villagers in their ignorance seized the horses. General Ba ordered his soldiers to arrest the villagers and try them as rebels; most were killed, and their wives and lands were confiscated by the government. Those who escaped the net abandoned their homes and fled, with no way to return, and scattered over the countryside. Then someone suddenly appeared to lead them, gathering the fugitives into bands and using the pretext of levying pay to raise a rebellion; in truth they plundered the good and peaceful people. Master Dazhao was afraid, and led his dharma dependents down from Baohua Mountain.

In the early part of the fourth month I reflected that however the local bandits might make trouble outside, the Vinaya institution of the summer retreat and pravāraṇā (also called “binding the summer,” that is, a time of seclusion) had long fallen into disuse within the temple and had never been observed. Now that I had newly become abbot, I explained to the assembly that cultivating the Way must accord with the Vinaya, and that since the summer had come round we could no longer put off the institution of the retreat and the closing ceremony. So on the sixteenth day of the fourth month we entered the earlier summer retreat. There were more than a hundred and sixty bhikshus and eight sramaneras, a hundred and seventy-three in all, and every one of them strictly observed the Vinaya rules and laboured with double their usual diligence.

When the twentieth day of the fifth month came, before daylight, the bandit chief Zhang Xiufeng came with more than a hundred men to the gate of the temple. As soon as the gate was opened they swarmed in and said to me: ‘This temple has many storied buildings and a great kitchen; lend us lodging for a few days.’ I said: ‘The rooms and the kitchen may be used, but there are two things that make it inconvenient. First, you demand pay from people, and if they do not give it you will certainly seize them and hang them up and beat and question them to exact it. We monks would look on, and both sides would be embarrassed. Second, if we monks eat from the same pot as you, and the authorities come to know of it, our guilt and calamity will be inescapable. I have heard that when Master Miaofeng first built this temple, the elders and countryfolk of the neighbouring villages all rejoiced and eagerly lent their labour, carrying the bricks, tiles, timber, and stone for the bronze hall; among them too was the merit of your fathers and grandfathers. If it is destroyed today, it is your own field of blessing that you destroy. There are many places to stay; you may go and seek elsewhere!’ Thus I declined again and again, until at last he said: ‘We will do as the Master says, and lodge outside the temple.’ It had not occurred to me that the resident monk Kexiu had a brother who was also a bandit chief and belonged to that very band, and that Kexiu often slipped out of the temple privately to visit him. When I asked him about the bandits’ doings he did not utter a word. The whole assembly was sick with anxiety, and he alone was utterly unconcerned. I said to the assembly: ‘Let each of you bring a bundle of firewood, and we will burn Kexiu to death, to cut off this great danger and protect the monastery.’ When he heard that, his soul nearly left him for fright, and he shut himself up in his room and would not come out. His teacher Jixian knelt on the ground weeping and begged me, willing to receive my correction and imploring that he be spared from burning. He at once called Kexiu to him, and I said to him: ‘At noon tomorrow the monastery will set out a vegetarian feast and invite ten of the leaders; not one more may come. If you can do this, your death is spared; but if more men enter the temple, or if they do not come, then you must still be burned.’

That evening I gathered everyone together and said: ‘At noon tomorrow, when the bandit chiefs come, let the whole temple form two ranks, left and right, the young in front and the old behind. Fear nothing and say nothing. Until I say “Go,” you all stand still; when I say “Go,” then all of you withdraw together. Leave only twenty men, two to attend at each seat.’

At noon they came as agreed. When they were seated, the monks formed two ranks. I said: ‘You gentlemen have risen today because your wives and families have been carried off and your lands and property confiscated by the government; and being all subjects of the Ming, you surely could not bear your wrongs in silence — you have acted because you had no choice.’ When they heard this, every man of them wept and said: ‘You are a man of understanding, Master; you know everything.’ Then I straightened up, struck the table with my hand, and said: ‘Today I have invited you to a vegetarian feast because this bronze hall was built by imperial decree and the Dragon Canon was bestowed by the Emperor. The monks cannot cultivate in peace and austerity — would you have the heart to destroy this monastery of a thousand years! That too is to act because there is no choice!’ When they saw me speak thus, they too turned pale with fright and answered again and again: ‘We understand, we understand! We know there are men among the monks both of letters and of arms. Pray do not be angry, Master; at dawn tomorrow we shall strike camp and go elsewhere.’ Then I soothed them with gentle words, and they took their leave and went out of the temple gate. Sure enough, at the fifth watch they struck camp and moved away. To guard against the government troops arriving suddenly at daybreak, I at once ordered the various officers to take lanterns and patrol every place carefully: if any ashes were left from cooking fires, they were to be swept up clean and covered with leaves; if there were feathers or bones of fowls and beasts, these were to be gathered up carefully and thrown into the deep ravine.

When the sky was near to light, the Zhenjiang garrison commander Lord Ma came up the mountain with troops and rode his horse straight into the temple, saying: ‘It has been established that the bandits lodged here eight days. Why did you shelter them and not report it to the authorities?’ I said: ‘Since they lodged here many days, there would be ashes left from their cooking fires, and feathers and bones left from the fowls and beasts they slaughtered and ate. Pray send men to look carefully in every place, and you will know.’ Men were sent to look, and they reported back that there was indeed no trace of any kind. He gave five taels of silver and went away. From that time the news that government troops had come to the temple spread abroad, and the donors and faithful all vanished from sight and dared not come up the mountain. Each day we had three meals of thin gruel, and for several days there was neither oil nor salt. The bandits came and went from time to time, and the monks who dwelt together were anxious and unsettled.

I said to the monks: ‘Today the summer retreat begins. Do not on any account give way to fear, for there are good spirits that secretly protect us! Whenever government troops or bandits come to the temple, I alone will step forward to answer them; the assembly need not be troubled to deal with them.’ When they heard this their minds grew calm again, and they applied themselves diligently to cultivation.

In the early part of the sixth month the bandits rose in great swarms and came up Baohua Mountain, some lodging in the Shangyuan Hermitage, some in the Longwo Hermitage, some in the Huanghua Cave Hermitage, some in the Lianxing Cliff Hermitage, some in the bridge pavilion, and some in the hermitage behind the kitchen. These six places all lie within the monastery’s boundary. Some of them wrote notes politely borrowing the monastery’s goods, while others, relying on the bandits’ power, sent men to demand them; I alone stepped forward and with flexible skill refused them. These men, the moment they heard the government troops were coming, fled and scattered beforehand, and when they learned the troops had gone they gathered again. I reckoned that if this went on it must bring down some great disaster. So I at once set the monks to work to pull down all the various hermitages and leave none standing.

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month I held the pravāraṇā (that is, the confession) in the abbot’s quarters. At that time Elder Yuan Yun was the western hall of this monastery, and he composed a poem on the dissolution of the retreat (by the Buddha’s rule, the summer retreat of dwelling in quiet ends on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, and this is called the dissolution of the retreat): Long buried lay the summer’s toil, / our Buddha’s rule, cold ash and soil; / white-headed monks no retreat kept — / Baohua’s Vinaya seat, new-swept. / The sticks we take match southern count, / the grass seats keep the West’s account; / pravāraṇā done — what wonder! / Upāli’s silenced lore roars thunder! (Upāli was one of the Buddha’s ten great disciples, honoured as foremost in upholding the precepts.)

In the early part of the eighth month the situation grew a little quieter. I entrusted the monastery’s affairs to the prior Dunwu and myself worshipped the Buddha alone in the abbot’s upper chamber. On the twelfth day I opened the window and looked out, and saw a middle-aged man, wearing an old blue robe above and with a bright red garment showing below, walking up and down under the eaves and peering about in every direction. I went down at once and said to Dunwu: ‘This man is a government soldier dressed as a layman, come to spy out the temple. On no account may he be allowed to stay.’ Dunwu quietly told the warden (the monk who patrols the monastery), and the warden said: ‘This is a man in the midst of trouble; let him stay over the Mid-Autumn Festival! Where can one not practise a little compassion?’ When I learned of it I called the warden and gave him a sharp scolding; and the man raised his head and looked at me. A little later more than a hundred bandits, each with a bamboo pole for a weapon, came and stood in a ring under the eaves of the cloister. At the sight Dunwu was greatly frightened; because he had been a eunuch, and everyone knew he was rich, he feared they would demand pay of him, so he pretended warm feeling, cooked rice, and entertained them, hoping to win them over. When I learned of it I came down at once; the bandits were already seated in the refectory, the bowls and chopsticks all laid out, and it seemed they could not be stopped. So I said to Dunwu: ‘The lives of more than a hundred in this temple and this ancient monastery of a thousand years are about to be ruined by this one meal of yours. If anything happens hereafter, the whole blame will be yours and nothing to do with me.’ That man with the red garment showing smiled and went away. The government general Ba, Lord Ao (
áo

) and Lord Chen the River Commandant (an official title) then led troops out of the city and cleared out the bandits, pitching their camp on the summit of East Xie Mountain. Only then did everyone understand that the man who had smiled and gone away had indeed been a scout sent by the government troops.

At midnight on the thirteenth more than a hundred Qing cavalry came up the mountain and threw a tight ring around Qianhua Temple. The assembly was in confusion, with no road of escape. At daybreak I said to Dunwu: ‘I am the abbot and you are the Steward. Now that trouble has come, we must bear it together. If the Qing troops enter the temple, the monastery will be stripped bare and the assembly will suffer with it.’ We opened the gate and came before the terrace of the bronze hall, and the officer leading the troops asked: ‘Which two are you?’ I answered: ‘The abbot and the Steward.’ The officer was pleased that we had come of ourselves to submit, and we went together to the temple gate and sat down. He asked how many monks were in the temple, and I answered: ‘Old and young together, ninety-four.’ The officer said: ‘Call them all out; whoever does not come out is a bandit.’ There were also carpenters, tilers, and image-makers working in the temple, and Dunwu called them all out as well. Among the soldiers was a bandit bound with ropes, who was made to identify people. He had been locked up a whole day and night, his wits scattered and his mind dull, and he could not speak, but only nodded at random. So when a craftsman stepped out, he nodded at him. In this way sixteen men were falsely accused of being bandits, and were at once seized, their necks lashed with ropes and their arms bound behind them, and taken away. Six others remained, and they too had ropes put round their necks and were marched off together to the army camp. When the official saw such laymen as these, he feared there might be others in hiding, so he sent two officers with four soldiers, ordering one soldier to guard the main gate, and told me and Dunwu to go into the temple with them. Wherever a cell was locked, they poked their fingers through the paper of the windows and peered inside. To keep them from suspicion I reached out, twisted the locks off, and opened the doors for them to see. They saw that the desks held nothing but sutras and that there were only beds besides. Two or three rooms were opened one after another, and all were the same; only then were they convinced that there was no deceit. For the other rooms that were locked, the officer would not let the locks be broken.

The officer came out of the temple gate and sat down, and said to me: ‘Someone has reported that you are hiding bandits in your temple. His Excellency has ordered us to seize them and take them to the army camp, not sparing old or young.’ He at once ordered one soldier on horseback to escort one monk in the rear, while he himself escorted me in front. I thought: with no one left in the temple and no one in command of the soldiers, if those soldiers in the rear were to crowd into the temple, then the monastery would be plundered until not a thing remained. So I said to the officer: ‘An officer leading troops marches in front to command his men when going into battle, and keeps to the rear to steady them when returning. I am the head of the monks and you are the officer of these soldiers; you should order the soldiers to escort the monks ahead, while you and I bring up the rear. Thus no monk will be missing and the soldiers will not get out of hand.’ The officer laughed and said: ‘Let it be as you say!’

After twenty li we reached the summit of East Xie Mountain and entered the great camp, where we saw countless bandits stripped naked and bound, and more than a thousand villagers crying out to heaven and weeping. A soldier holding a flag led us to squat down in one place, and the sixteen who had been wronged were brought up and questioned, then after a while led away again. Behind us we heard a soldier say: ‘You elders must all speak the truth. If you do not speak the truth, you will be like these sixteen and have your heads cut off!’ When he had spoken, we heard a sound, and all sixteen were killed; the other six were spared death. The blood of the slain splashed and stained our robes. I said to the assembly: ‘Do not on any account panic; let every man single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. If this is fixed karma from many lives, then today it must be repaid. If we are not within this kalpa of doom, we shall of course be delivered. The strength of one’s daily practice is shown precisely at such a time as this.’ And all of them murmured the Buddha’s name.

The county magistrate Chen came down, and Dunwu alone was called up and put to torture. He testified that I was the abbot. Soldiers were then sent to call me. I thought that birth and death are like foam on water, rising and perishing, and that in the face of calamity a monk must not lose his dignity; so I walked slowly and straight up. The soldiers ranged on either side held drawn swords and shouted all together in menace, ordering me to kneel. I said sternly: ‘I wear the Tathagata’s robe, and the Buddha’s rule does not permit me to bow to a layman. How could I kneel on the ground to beg for my life and deliberately break the Vinaya!’ I joined my palms, bowed my body in a single salute of inquiry, and stood to one side. General Ba pointed at me and laughed, rubbed his own forehead, held up a thumb, and spoke at length in Manchu to General Ao and Lord Chen the River Commandant. The interpreter translated for me: ‘Lord Ba says the crown of your head is the same as His Lordship’s; you are a good monk, and he does not require you to kneel.’ Lord Chen the River Commandant asked me: ‘The bandits lodged long on Baohua Mountain — why did you not report it by night and day, but instead sheltered them without authority?’ I said: ‘High as Baohua Mountain is, there is a great road for travellers over its summit. If the bandits went up the front of the mountain and down the back, those in front would see them and say they were lodging on Baohua. If they passed from the back to the front, those behind would see them and say they were lodging on Baohua. Had I come to report it, there would have been no bandits to seize, and the fault would have fallen on me instead. It is not that I sheltered them and did not report. Baohua Mountain is right before your eyes; pray look at it yourself, Your Excellency.’ The River Commandant turned his head and looked up, and indeed there was a great road over the mountain. He said: ‘Then this matter will not be pursued. Now I ask you: the eunuch Sun was an inner official of the Ming and privately kept bandits, harbouring rebellion in his heart — you must have known of it.’ I said: ‘The eunuch Sun came up the mountain to leave home in the sixteenth year of Chongzhen. He has been prior less than half a year. I know only that he gave up office to cultivate; whether his intentions were good or ill is a secret matter — how could I know it!’ The River Commandant said: ‘That is indeed a secret matter; no doubt you do not know it either. Go down!’ And I went down as slowly as before.

Above, Dunwu was again tortured and questioned about giving food to the bandits, and he in turn dragged Kexiu into it. The two men pushed the blame back and forth and would not admit it, and Kexiu too had his feet clamped in the torture press and was whipped. Unable to bear the pain, he also testified that I was the abbot and master of the temple. They came to call me again, and I said to the monks: ‘This time I go, I fear I may not return. Let all of you set your minds right and not be frightened on my account.’ As before, I went up calmly, joined my palms, bowed, and stood there. The River Commandant said: ‘In your temple, on the twelfth, you gave the bandits winter-melon rice to eat. I already have men who inquired into it clearly in the temple — why conceal it?’ I saw Kexiu’s feet clamped in the press and Dunwu bound and kneeling beside him, and I rebuked them both, saying: ‘It is plain that on the twelfth more than a hundred men came to the temple and did eat winter-melon rice — why not admit it? You have put Their Excellencies to the trouble of questioning you again and again, and brought this great suffering on yourselves.’ The River Commandant laughed and said: ‘You are truly a good man. Speak straight out to me!’

I said: ‘Is Your Excellency asking about the meals given over the years, or only about the meal on the twelfth, yesterday?’ The River Commandant said: ‘What is this about meals over the years?’ I said: ‘The villages within a hundred li around are all together called Baohua. The temple has many monks, and every year at the two harvests, summer and autumn, we must go to each village to beg grain and wheat, so every village is a donor. When they come to the temple, no matter how many they are, we must entertain them with tea and food. If we did not entertain them, next year we should beg no grain. From the building of the bronze hall down to today it has been so every year — not only the one meal on the twelfth of the eighth month this year. They came to the temple without bows and arrows or weapons; how could one know which was a bandit and which was not?’ The River Commandant spoke a while in Manchu to Lords Ba and Ao, and the interpreter translated for me: ‘Their three Excellencies say you are a straightforward man who does not speak falsely; the matter of the meals will not be pursued. You may go down!’

Above they next questioned Dunwu about the property the monastery possessed. Fearing torture, he reported to the officials everything — fields, lands, mountain holdings, and all the rest. He also said that the silver and money and the treasury were in the charge of Fohui, and that only he would know. So men were sent to call Fohui for questioning. He answered that the treasury held only thirty-six taels of silver and eight or nine thousand coppers. The officials did not believe it and flew into a rage, bound Fohui and beat him. He could not answer, and said the abbot knew. The county magistrate came down to call me. Lords Ba and Ao, seeing that I had come and gone several times without disorder in my step or change in my face, said a few words to the interpreter, and the interpreter said to me: ‘His Excellency tells you to sit down and speak; do not be afraid!’ Lord Chen the River Commandant said: ‘The temple on Baohua is great and the monks are many; the daily expenses cannot be small. Why falsely report only thirty-six taels of silver?’ I said: ‘The keeper of the treasury was frightened and could not speak clearly.’ He asked me again: ‘How much is there in fact?’ I said: ‘My own Master, Monk Sanmei, had vast karmic connections; many princes, marquises, and officials took refuge with him, and there was a great deal of silver. But he was a man of free and easy ways who kept not a coin for himself, building temples and making Buddha images everywhere. In his last year he rebuilt Baohua Mountain and used up all the money. He passed away in the intercalary sixth month of last year. We who are his disciples are thin in merit and lacking in conditions, and money and grain are scarce, while the monks are many and the monastery short of what it needs. The temple once had a black horse, which was sold to Lord Che of the Nanjing Imperial Weaving Office for fifty-eight taels of silver. On the eighth or ninth of last month twenty-two taels were spent, and so only thirty-six remain. If Your Excellency does not believe it, send a man to ask Lord Che, and you will know the truth!’ The three Lords Ba, Ao, and Chen talked together a while and all nodded. The interpreter said to me: ‘Their three Excellencies say you have not spoken falsely, and they will not send to ask Lord Che.’ Then they loosened the ropes that bound Fohui. Next they called up Xuanwen and Jixuan. The River Commandant said: ‘I have learned that you two, like Kexiu, are local men who left home here and belong to a branch household of Baohua; bind them!’ Then the River Commandant said to me: ‘The business of these four men is nothing to do with you. Go down!’ I dared not look back again, but came down and sat with the monks.

When noon came, the sun blazed down and scorched us, and there was no tree to give shade. We had sat there a long while, hungry, every man drenched with sweat and hardly able to endure it. Suddenly a patch of dark cloud flew over and covered the sky above us like a great canopy, while light still shot out from its edges. As the sky gradually darkened a soldier came carrying a flag and said in a loud voice: ‘Elders all, follow me.’ I thought we were going to be tortured, and every face changed colour. But there were kindly men in the camp too: one joined his palms joyfully and said aloud: ‘Masters all, you are saved! Before, the black flag was set over you and you were certain to die. Now it has been changed to the green flag — so do not be afraid, set your hearts at rest!’ I looked up and indeed it was the green flag, and only then did everyone’s heart find peace.

The soldier with the flag led us to the foot of a hillside, where we all sat down on the ground. Several dozen soldiers stood around watching us and said: ‘If it were not for this abbot here, who came and went several times and argued the matter clear — and he has the good fortune to be in the favour of Their three Excellencies — not one of you would be alive today.’ One soldier came up to me and said: ‘You have toiled all day; now take a breath!’ And he unfastened the quiver from his waist and gave it to me for a pillow. I said: ‘That is a weapon of killing; a man who keeps the precepts does not use it.’ Another soldier said: ‘You must be hungry!’ And he at once offered me a dry cake he carried with him. I took the cake, broke it into small pieces, and gave each man a piece. He said: ‘Eat it yourself — do not share it!’ I said: ‘We who dwell and cultivate together go hungry together when hungry and eat together when there is food. And now, in the midst of calamity, can we do anything but share alike!’ All the soldiers standing around admired it greatly. Among themselves they agreed: ‘Let us go to the village ahead and cook some food and bring it at dawn tomorrow.’ At midnight we were tormented with thirst, and seeing a small pool below the slope, we all ran over and drank, and it tasted sweet and cool. When day broke and we looked, it was a filthy wallow where cattle had lain.

After the sun came up a soldier came and led me into the camp tent. Lord Chen the River Commandant said to me: ‘You are a man of cultivation; you may preside over Baohua and lead the monks back.’ I said: ‘I will not dwell there now.’ The River Commandant said to the assembly: ‘Since he will not dwell there, choose another from among you, a man of good conduct, to preside.’ The assembly answered with one voice: ‘Only this abbot can preside; there is no one else to do it.’ Lord Chen laughed and said: ‘I tell you to dwell there and the assembly also chooses you. Why did you preside before and will not now?’ I said: ‘The reason I presided before was that my late Master had passed away and the pagoda was not finished. Had I abandoned it and gone because the bandits made trouble, men everywhere would have accused me of unfilial conduct, and so I did not leave. The reason I will not dwell there now is that more than a hundred monks were wrongfully seized and brought here, and only through the clear discernment of Their three Excellencies were they spared from death — it is life given back after death. Besides, Baohua has become a land of calamity: if the bandits still pass back and forth over the mountain and someone again reports that we are sheltering them, will not the monks once more sit waiting for death? Therefore I will not be abbot again. And even if the pagoda is not finished, there is no crime of unfilial conduct in it.’ The River Commandant said: ‘You need not wear yourself out refusing out of concern for what may come later. Lords Ba and Ao and I will be your Dharma protectors; Baohua Mountain is the incense and fire of this dynasty, and no soldiers will ever again come to trouble it. Henceforth, if soldiers or others come to the temple to do harm or make trouble, you need only send in a note and I will have them seized and beheaded. Tomorrow I shall give you a proclamation to take back and post in the temple.’ I said: ‘Today I will obey and go back to dwell there. But the eunuch Sun reported all the monastery’s fields, lands, and mountain holdings to the authorities, and they were confiscated. They were not his private property; I beg that they be returned to the monks of the monastery.’ The River Commandant was pleased, and returned everything. So I and the assembly gave thanks and went back to the temple.

When I came into the hall to worship the Buddha, I could not keep back my grief and desolation; I fell prostrate on the ground and my tears would not cease. By what karma have I been granted again to gaze upon my Buddha’s golden countenance! The Daoist Chen of Yanxiang Village below the mountain was a disciple who had taken refuge; when he heard that on the night of the thirteenth the Qing troops had surrounded the temple and carried all the monks off to the camp, he was greatly worried. On the fifteenth he wished to come up the mountain to see us, and his son and nephew urged him: ‘The camp is still on East Xie Mountain; the whole countryside is strewn with corpses and the roads are emptied of travellers. Do not go so soon!’ He said: ‘This disciple knows his Master is in danger — would you have me sit by and look on!’ He reached the temple at noon, saw that all the monks had been released, and asked how it had gone; when I had told him the whole story from beginning to end, he went home easy and glad at heart. At this time Acharya Xiangxue was opening a period at Shangfang Temple in Zhenjiang. The brothers Chunzhi went to Zhenjiang to buy incense and candles, and putting up for the night at Shangfang Temple they saw Master Xiang. Master Xiang said: ‘Trouble has come to Baohua; do not let it involve my period-hall. You may go and lodge elsewhere.’ The Chunzhi brothers came out with tears in their eyes and returned to the temple on the eighteenth, and told us what had happened. When the assembly heard it, they all sighed without end. I said: ‘Baohua Mountain is the place where the old Master’s whole-body su (
sū
) du, that is, “sudu,” a transliteration of the Sanskrit
stūpa

, meaning a Buddha pagoda, stands. When it was said to be in trouble, not only did he neither ask after it nor heed it, but when he saw those who had come back alive he neither pitied them nor kept them. What kind of heart is my Master Xiang’s! And what kind of feeling is that of the Daoist Chen!’

Half a month later a stout fellow whose dress suggested he belonged to the army camp came to the temple. The assembly, like birds startled by the bow, were all greatly frightened at the sight of him. I went up to him and questioned him mildly. He said: ‘I have been sent by His Excellency the River Commandant to fetch a horse.’ I said: ‘There is indeed a good horse in the temple; you may ride it away!’ He was delighted to hear it. Then I said: ‘The horse may be given you, but have you any warrant?’ He took a small note from his waist and handed it to me. I saw that it was not signed in vermilion but in red earth. I took the note, and cried out in a loud voice: ‘Which band are you a local bandit from, that you dare come to the temple to extort a horse by fraud! Have you not heard that Their Excellencies Ba, Ao, and Chen are the Dharma protectors of Baohua? Bind him and send him to the authorities!’ At once he dropped to the ground with a thud, knocked his head on the floor and begged for mercy, saying: ‘I was unwilling to come; it was our chief Zhang Kun who sent me!’ And he wept without ceasing. Suddenly it came on to rain hard, and I pitied him too, and said: ‘Today I will let you go. If you ever do such a thing again, you will not be spared! Here is a pair of straw sandals and an umbrella — be off!’ He pulled off his leather boots, put on the sandals, and went off at speed through the rain. From that time Baohua Mountain was at peace and the bandits vanished.

In the second month of the sixth year of Shunzhi, one or two of Master Dazhao’s disciples — I was their Precept-Instructing Master — deliberately flouted the monastic rules, and when Master Da learned of it he was indulgent instead and gave them no admonition. So I came down from the mountain and crossed the river, intending to go to the northern Wutai. When I reached Guanshan in Chuzhou I met Master Zhanyi, the Steward of that temple, who kept me there in the temple and begged me to transmit the precepts to him. Elder Yuan Yun was a disciple ordained by the late Master, Monk Sanmei, who had shaved his head; I too had been his Precept-Instructing Master, and he was then studying the Vinaya on Baohua Mountain. He gathered the assembly in the late Master’s portrait hall (the hall where Monk Sanmei is honoured), instructed and rebuked the dharma dependents dwelling in the temple, and said to Master Dazhao: ‘The Monk Jian is the successor abbot charged by the late Master to his face, and he preserved the monastery out of deadly peril. By right you ought to observe the precepts, heed his teaching, and follow him in earnest cultivation. Why do you resist and disobey him, provoke him to anger, and so destroy your own house? Today in offending the abbot you offend the late Master!’ He wrote out the notice of expulsion with his own hand (the announcement by which a monk who has broken a grave precept is expelled from the temple) and drove the lawless men out of the temple. Master Dazhao, having invited the great worthy Liyan to join him, came to Guanshan in Chuzhou and brought me back to Baohua Mountain. The Vinaya rules were again strictly enforced, and only then was an ordination platform established for transmitting the full precepts. No fewer than three thousand came to seek ordination; the grain stored in the temple was enough for only a few days, and even so the daily meals were never cut off.

In the winter of the sixth year of Shunzhi the president of the Long Life Society of Ningguo Prefecture came to invite me, and I agreed to consider it later. The seventh year of Shunzhi was my fiftieth birthday. Donors from the four quarters came of themselves in throngs to make offerings, and the venerable elders of high repute from the various temples also graciously came in person to Baohua. There was a Master Mixin, shaved and ordained by the late Master and also the Master of Witness who had presided at my own full ordination, who now contended for the abbacy of Baohua Mountain. On the morning of the fifteenth day of the fourth month I struck the gavel and gathered the assembly in the abbot’s quarters, inviting Master Mi to be present as well. I said to them: ‘From ancient times the abbot has always been respectfully invited from among men of virtue. This humble one is thin in virtue and unfit to occupy this seat. Today, before the assembly, I have reckoned up clearly the money and grain that have come in and gone out of the monastery, and I hand them over to Master Mi to manage. There are at present more than three hundred piculs of rice in store, more than two hundred taels of silver, and over ninety thousand coppers.’ From these I took fifty-two thousand coppers and distributed them to the assembly. The oil, salt, fruit, and other stores in the treasury were enough for a year’s use. Having entrusted everything to Master Mi, I moved into the east tower to live and no longer concerned myself with any internal affair. The next day, the sixteenth, I made all arrangements with the assembly for the earlier summer retreat. On the sixteenth (probably the seventeenth) I made an incense offering at the late Master’s pagoda and bowed in farewell. The Vinaya provides that when conditions of difficulty arise, a man may be permitted to move elsewhere for the summer retreat, so I said to the assembly: ‘Tomorrow morning I am going to the Long Life Society in Ningguo Prefecture for the summer retreat.’ The assembly came to tell me that they all wished to leave the mountain with me. I said: ‘Baohua Mountain was restored to prosperity when the late Master changed the temple’s orientation, and it is the place where the late Master entered nirvāṇa and where his pagoda was built; it is the ancestral court of our Vinaya school, and I would gladly be its sweeper and servant forever, but the conditions are what they are. Now let us consider together: whoever is willing to keep watch over the ancestral court in my place and is resolved on austere cultivation, let him stand on the left — it will be no harm if we meet again later. Whoever is determined to come down the mountain with me, let him stand on the right.’

When the assembly heard this they divided into two sides. Those who would go down the mountain with me were the greater part, more than a hundred men. At dawn on the eighteenth the deputy prior (deputy steward) Lüzhong offered us thirty taels of silver for travelling expenses, and I smiled and would not take it. He said: ‘This is an incense offering given by the faithful to the abbot (meaning Master Jianyue), not an offering to the monks at large.’ I said: ‘If it is all handed over, what difference is there?’ After breakfast we came down the mountain. When we reached Laopeng Bridge we met the Daoist Zhang, who invited us to a vegetarian meal and hired a boat to carry us. At night we lodged at the Two Loyalists Shrine at Xiaguan, where the Steward was a disciple of mine in the precepts; he kept us three days, and no small number of the faithful came to take refuge, sending altogether more than forty piculs of rice and incense offerings amounting to a hundred taels. Then we hired a boat and went upstream, and only at the very end of the fourth month did we reach Ningguo. Our host received us with great warmth.

In the early part of the fifth month two or three disciples came after us in haste from Baohua Mountain. According to them, after I came down the mountain the magistrate of Jurong County learned that Master Mixin had contended for the abbacy and that I had yielded the abbot’s seat and gone down, whereupon he summoned Master Mi to the lower house at Longtan, rebuked him soundly, and required him to bring me back within half a month. Afterwards the Dharma protector Chen Min (
mín

)zhao came up the mountain to worship the Buddha, and when he heard this news he wept aloud and said to the assembly: ‘The abbot of this mountain has gone and the monastery has fallen at once into decline. The root of the trouble is not Mixin alone; it is only because his dependents stirred him up that such a thing could happen. By rights they should be sent to the yamen for severe punishment, but for the present I will pardon you. Since I am a Dharma protector, my first concern is to protect the jewel of the Sangha; I shall choose a day and go myself to Xuancheng to bring the abbot back to the mountain.’ On the twenty-first day of the seventh month the Dharma protector Chen reached Xuancheng and told me the whole story of his visit to the mountain and his coming to fetch me. In my heart I was deeply moved by the sincerity of his protection and felt ashamed. On the twenty-fourth I ordered the assembly to go aboard the boats and return to the mountain, while I and the Dharma protector Chen went back by the overland road. On the twenty-ninth we reached Jiangning. The next day Monk Juelang (whose dharma name was Daosheng; he once presided over the Tianjie Temple in Jinling and the Chongguang Temple in Hangzhou and other great places of practice, whereby the wind of the Chan school was greatly revived; see the Record of Pure Land Sages and Worthies, Easy Explanation) and the Dharma protector Chen Minzhao and the others escorted me all together into Baohua Mountain. On the way, when we reached Fanjiachang, night was falling, and the villagers, hearing that I was returning to the mountain, men and women alike vied to see me, while others carried torches and followed us all along the road, so that the light was as bright as day. Monk Juelang laughed aloud and said: ‘A wondrous sight! A wondrous sight!’ And he said to the Dharma protectors: ‘That Master Jian’s dwelling on the mountain should have such an influence and such an effect as this! Truly it is a good omen that the Dharma way is about to flourish greatly!’

The next day I gathered the officers of the various halls who had stayed behind on the mountain and discussed preparing a feast to thank the various protectors of the Dharma. I asked what the monastery still kept in store. The prior, Ruojian, replied: ‘There is no silver or money at all; of rice there are only a few measures left, and the storehouses are wholly empty.’ I sighed and said: ‘I have been away from the mountain not yet five months; how has the monastery come to such a pass?’ Ruojian said: ‘After the master left, the mountain was no longer like a Vinaya hall; everyone was thinking of going off elsewhere. And Master Mishi, every day, enjoyed sumptuous offerings (eating the best) with nothing coming in, and so what was stored has been used up. It is like using a limited supply of dead water, lacking a living spring, and so we have come to this state. And as for me, I could not decide anything.’ When the protectors heard this, they all knit their brows and were very displeased at heart. I said: ‘This return to the monastery is indeed very different from my return from the army camp last time. Simply go along with conditions; there is no need to worry!’ Gradually, people from near and far who came seeking the precepts grew more and more. I said to them: ‘The mountain is thin and poor and bitter. To add people to feed, we can only add a ladle of water; there is no rice to add. Those who cannot endure this hardship, please go elsewhere.’ They all were willing to stay on the mountain, and not one went elsewhere. From the eighth year of the Shunzhi reign, in every winter and summer season, the assembly within and without gathered together in one hall, reciting the Buddha-name for seven days and seven nights without pause, still eating only one bowl of gruel at midday, with no further meal after noon. This rule has been handed down and followed ever since, without change. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the day of self-reflection, in accordance with the scriptural regulations and ritual, an Ullambana offering was set up, and all the abbot’s money and goods were distributed in full to the assembly, to repay the profound kindness of parents — established as a constant and unchanging rule.

In the ninth year of the Shunzhi reign, the land south of the Yangtze suffered locusts and drought; not a blade of grass grew, and the common people went hungry and starving. The old and young, men and women, of the villages all came up the mountain seeking food. They were not entirely beggars; among them were also those who held fields, and at one go they came in groups of one or two hundred. I told the sangha to reduce their own rations to relieve them. One day around noon, the number who came was several times the usual, and the halls, courtyards, and corridors were filled with people. I seized the opportunity to instruct them, saying: ‘Everyone today, having no alternative, has come up the mountain. Each of you should look at the causes from the past. Because in former lives you did not believe in the Three Jewels, and being miserly and greedy were unwilling to give alms to the poor, you have drawn upon yourselves today’s retribution. Today I shall gather contributions from the assembly and give each of you three coins. I too shall give each of you one coin of my own. You must all recite the Buddha-name in your mouths and receive this with both hands, to make offering on your behalf and to plant a pure field of merit, so that in the future you may all be free from the suffering of poverty.’ Having thus taught them, at once the sound of the Buddha-name rose like thunder. I then ordered a monk to sweep the storehouse completely clean; the rice obtained was cooked into a meal, and after everyone had eaten his fill at will, they all went off reciting the Buddha-name. By this, the monastery had no rice left even for the following morning. On the next morning there was only a pot of plain boiled water for the meal, and by evening the layman Huang Junfu of Jiangning sent ten measures of rice to the mountain.

In the middle of the second month of the tenth year, a nun of Hanyang Prefecture in Chuzhou named Xinwen, already fifty years old and resolved to observe the precepts, led her nine disciples on a boat, fearing neither the distance nor the dangers of the road, and came to Huashan. The ten of them entered the monastery and begged for three months’ residence, offering sixty measures of rice and twenty taels of silver. Seeing that their intent was sincere and their words earnest, I took pity and consented. When the day came to set out a feast and offer to the assembly, she would not enter the hall to bow to the monks. When the meal was over, I gathered the assembly, had her called, and said: ‘You have roused your heart to come from afar to learn the precepts. Why do you not enter the dining hall and bow to the monks? The Vinaya rule stipulates that a bhikshuni, even at the age of a hundred, should bow to a bhikshu of the first summer (a bhikshu who received the full precepts only a year ago). Today you yourself are arrogant and haughty, showing great disrespect toward the monks — this is not the conduct of one who studies the precepts.’ She said: ‘Wherever I have been, in the Chu region, if there were a good spiritual friend, I would go and set a feast and offer to the assembly. The abbots there all treated me with the courtesy of a guest, and did not require me to bow.’ I said: ‘They are greedy for offerings and are corrupting the Dharma. Seeing a nun who can make offerings, they honor her as their own mother, wishing to obtain even more abundant offerings. They are worms in the lion’s body, not true spiritual friends. Though Huashan at present is thin and poor and bitter, I would rather run out of grain and miss meals than dare to violate the Vinaya rules to seek gain. The feast set up today may be counted for the monastery’s own use. The silver spent I return to you in full; and the rice you brought, place it in the lower courtyard and take it away with you. Go elsewhere!’ Not understanding the principle, she took the silver, led her disciples, went down the back mountain, and lodged in the quiet room of the Water-Out Cave. At this a disciple, Gutang, came to the abbot’s room and said: ‘She has come from afar, and the monastery’s storehouse is empty. Master, exercise a little kindness and take her in. For one thing, it keeps her from losing her resolve for the Way; for another, the assembly will have half a month’s provisions.’ My face darkened and I said: ‘If one is willing to practice truly, the assembly will naturally not go hungry with hanging bowls. To establish the Dharma, it should be precisely in such a time of bitter poverty and hardship, in word and deed. A Vinaya master carrying out the precepts — can he violate the holy ordinances for the sake of gain?’ Gutang, blushing, bowed and withdrew.

After three days, the nun Xinwen again led her disciples up the mountain, and they all knelt outside the abbot’s door, weeping and saying: ‘When we were in Chu we were truly befuddled to such a degree — it was really our own arrogance and slighting of the monks. We humbly beg the master, out of his compassion, to allow us to repent. From now on, all your teaching and instruction we shall follow and carry out one by one!’ The heads of the various halls also pleaded on their behalf. Therefore I had them go to the Deer-Mountain Manor, where a boundary was drawn for them to carry out the summer residence, and I dispatched an acarya and others to go there every half-month to give them instruction, and to explain for them the fundamental Vinaya text of our order. From this matter onward, I formed the resolve to compile the one scroll, The Proper Standard for Instructing Bhikshunis, and to circulate it.

In the first part of the eighth month, the monk Huiyi of the rear hall, a man of the Chu region who had long studied in the Chan school, came up the mountain to rely upon me, studying the precepts. One day the monastery brought out the stored scriptures to air them. Huiyi turned the leaves of the Sutra of the Pratyutpanna Samadhi. The next day he said to me: ‘The Pratyutpanna Samadhi in the scriptures is the essential substance of pure-karma practice, and the hardest of all to carry out.’ I said: ‘Earlier, at the five platforms of the north, I too heard a good spiritual friend instruct that to practice the Pratyutpanna Samadhi one must not sit or lie down, but must stand for ninety days. Later, coming to this place, I read the Collected Conduct of the Vinaya Ancestor Daoxuan of the Southern Mountain and learned that the ancestral master had long practiced this method, and that after him, those who practiced it became few. If one can only let go of the body, naturally one can do it.’ So I fixed the twentieth day of the eighth month as the start, and in the abbot’s room, emulating the worthies of old, I practiced the ninety days; I made a vow to follow in the footsteps of the patriarchs, declining all affairs and entering the retreat. Having completed the term on the twenty-first day of the eleventh month, I again, in the autumn of the twelfth year of the Shunzhi reign, practiced ninety days a second time. I rejoice that I had such good conditions as to let me plant this pure cause twice. Yet I am deeply ashamed of my heavy hindrances, and that I did not gain deep benefit.

As for my relying on the Vinaya rules to reform some of the earlier expedient methods and to hold them strictly in accordance with the Dharma; and my compiling the Proper Standard of the Vinaya to distinguish what is false and spread it abroad; and all these matters of the conditions for guiding and transforming beings; as well as establishing a precept altar to transmit the precepts, setting an example for later generations; purchasing field and mountain to support the sangha; and all the various works of building, great and small — all these undertakings were to complete and enrich the plans that the former elder could not finish after he redirected his course. By these I repay his profound kindness to me in bestowing upon me the milk of the Dharma of the precepts. This is also the real substance of my decades of painstaking effort, with an iron spine bearing up to sustain the Buddha’s work of spreading the Dharma. Here, not fearing to be tediously long-winded, I have set it before you all, one item after another. These are all things that the acarya Liyan and the great disciples who long attended me witnessed with their own eyes. But one must know that all that has form returns to illusion. Now, recalling the former events, it is only a dream; therefore I have titled it A Wandering Talk of a Dream. I add a gatha:
A dream southward for many a year, through peril and hardship I came;
And now you ask of my southern route — I answer still in a dream’s own frame.
